comments.name: Laurence
comments.body:
Hello, Mr. Burns.
I'm afraid that you are a bit too cheerful about the American
past.
John Adams and Alexander Hamilton both helped write the 
Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798.
The Alien Act helped deport foreigners who, in their opinion,
took the wrong stance on the French Revolution, and about the war between England and France.
And the Sedition Act helped president Adams to shut down 
newspapers he didn't like, and place some of their editors in
prison.
Sound familiar?
Thomas Jefferson stopped that, but still had an estate full of slaves.  And in the 1820's, the US approved of France extorting money from Haiti, to pay for the freed slaves.  For a century and a half.
MAYBE we'll get lucky these days.  But recoveries usually occur
following a great catastrophe.  Like the Renaissance coming after the Black Plague of 1347.
Up next?  A climate and economic crisis coming together.  Trump has pretty much assured us of those.

It's been clear to me for 10 years that he's more than a misogynist. He's a misanthrope. He hates people in theory. He treats them like the flagpoles he hugs as if that proves patriotism but is actually "objectifying" America. comments.name: Joshua Kline
comments.body:
Hopefully, the Democratic rout is less about the cost of a fill-up than about decency—or, in Trump's case, increasingly, indecency.  One is temporary and policy-driven; the other once represented the nation's very essence.
   Notably, Trump's $5000 "If we win" cash giveaway, the $500 Obamacare bribe, and even Musk's billions failed to flip the flop.
All the king's horses and all the king's men couldn't put Trumpy together again. Is this the end of America's decline, or a bump in the road?  It is easier to break something thant to put it together.

   Now, at least, with Trump already boasting about his veto power, the world can prepare for two years of irresolution, but at least it is the right kind of irresolution.  The courts will be busier than ever.
 
   Are we seeing a rejection of the fundamental indecency which the president increasingly manifests, a turn among the electorate to traditional human values, or a reaction to the cost of a tank-full?

   Most Canadians hope that this rejection represents an awakening, a return to the values for which America once stood.  But even if Trumpism is dying, Trump is alive, soon to be regarded as the Obstructionist-in-Chief.  This election enlivened the American vision while rejecting vicious opportunism.  It is the first step on a long, slow road toward Making America Great Again.

comments.name: Jorge Sanchez
comments.body:
Parents have a choice about how their children are educated, whether in public, private or faith-based schools. I respect that freedom. But being gay is not a choice. Gay parents cannot choose to be straight to satisfy a religious institution. Their only alternative is to hide who they are, denying their true nature and dignity.

Religious schools have the right to uphold their beliefs. But when they accept taxpayer dollars, should they also have the right to exclude children because their parents are gay? Public funding comes from families of every background, including those being excluded. Religious freedom deserves protection, but so does equal treatment.

I say this as a gay man who was once deeply devoted to his Catholic faith. As I grew older, I experienced painful rejection and was made to feel unwelcome. I eventually left, not because I rejected the Christian teachings of love and compassion, but because I could no longer reconcile those teachings with how I was treated.

I recognize that many Catholics welcome LGBTQ+ families. My objection is not to religious education, but to using public funds to support discrimination. Educational choice should expand opportunities, not make some families feel less worthy simply because of who they are.

comments.name: GabI Mir
comments.body:
Trump is finished .. PERIOD 

Let's see how he will get out from the scene !

comments.name: R Murphy
comments.body: The WSJ EB asked, “Will Democrats learn the wrong lesson from this win?”   Answer…..probably.  Of course, they will be enabled to DJT himself.  Unless he does what he has proven incapable of doing in the past, and that is ‘learn his lesson’…he’ll continue to blame and alienate others.  It’ll be a rough 2. Years for all of us. As I often comment to my liberal friends (…and my lib wife), don’t worry…..the Mid-terms will fix what’s ailing us.  …and they did.  Did I like it?  No.  Did I expect it?  Yes.  Will both Dems and Reps learn?  That’s the great unknown.  Trump surely deserves what’s coming to him…..but if history is any lesson, Dems will over-reach and underperform.  Then…wash/rinse/repeat.

comments.name: Valued Reader
comments.body:
Democrats have a once in a lifetime opportunity…. 

First, move to the CENTER.  

Second, remove Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jefferies from leadership roles.  

Third, place tight controls on spending and borrowing (national debt and federal deficit).

Tenth, vote to stop Trump’s rape of national landmarks…. White House “ballroom”, Kennedy Center, La Arch of Defeat, Golf Course, etc.

comments.name: Will B
comments.body: A president who doesn't understand this election was a massive rebuke of his accomplishment and lipstick, probably isn't mentally capable of serving his or its last two years.

comments.name: James Thorleifson
comments.body:
““LAWYER UP,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D., Calif.) posted on social media as it became clear Democrats were going to control the House. Garcia is likely to chair the House Oversight Committee and have broad powers to investigate the Trump administration. Sen. Ron Wyden (D., Ore.) posted “Subpoenas.””“Democracy is the theory that the common people know what they want, and deserve to get it good and hard.” - H.L. Mencken 

I don’t whether Mr. Mencken ended up above, or below, but wherever his shade rests, he’s having a good laugh this morning. 😉

comments.name: David S
comments.body: This was a repudiation of out of control hyperpartisanship, not just of Trump. Republicans won the governor's office in Vermont but not Texas. It's no coincidence that the GOP got clobbered the most heavily in places like Texas and North Carolina where Republicans knocked out their own incumbent Senators for being too independent of Trump, and where the GOP pursued aggressive gerrymanders. Voters saw a party that was out of control and slapped it down. Conversely, Democratic overperformance was far stronger in states where their candidate choices have consistently signaled "mainstream" (like in Iowa, Kansas, and North Carolina) than where voters have seen local Democrats nominate ideologues (like in Oregon, Minnesota, and Michigan).

comments.name: Chris
comments.body:
I remember when Reagan was first elected a gloating Republican spokesman making a prediction into a microphone that the country was headed into a future of a government run by the Republican party without any meaningful opposition parties and thinking, "Well, isn't that the Soviet Union?
That was over forty years ago. While the GOP has fallen short of achieving that since, the effort to do so has remained and taken full flower in the thinking of a former Democrat.

comments.name: WhiskeyTangoFoxtrot
comments.body:
"But the crusade has so far resulted in the Trump administration’s charging only about 236 people with voting-fraud-related offenses across the country since the president took office, according to the Justice Department’s tally on Monday afternoon."

And those are charges, not convictions.  This administration's charges are so flimsy I'd wager that one half to three-quarters of that 236 were charged based on mistakes made by our government.

There is not, and has never been, such a thing as widespread voter fraud, involving non-citizens or not, in the United States.  Period.

comments.name: Gandalfthegrey
comments.body: In all conspiracy theories (as opposed to scientific theories), the former START with the "theory" and then searches for supporting evidence.  It never finds any - despite costly, lengthy and goal-shifting strategies. The current voter fraud conspiracy is a prime example of fact-free dogma driving out rational thought -- very much like the Salem Witch Trials.

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body: Of those 236 people charged, how many were ACTUAL voters? I've read reports that some of those charged were legal voters. So that miniscule number will actually be smaller. Republicans say "even one" fraudulent vote is an attack on democracy. Yet Republicans want to disenfranchise tens of thousands of people -- the SAVE Act would disenfranchise millions -- because of a negligible number of fraudulent votes? And somehow disenfranchising legal voters isn't an attack on democracy? Of course it is. And of course that's the end goal: preserving Republican power.

comments.name: Russell ***********************

Wouldn’t it be interesting to know how much - $1 billion dollars wouldn’t surprise me.

comments.name: Michele
comments.body: The fact that the Trump regime continues to manufacture false accusations of voter fraud and has attempted to preemptively discredit the 2026 election is proof of two things. If you say something loudly enough and long enough it starts to gain credibility because it is everywhere polluting the airwaves. Second, innumeracy still reigns supreme among MAGA adherents.

comments.name: MP
comments.body: So, barring evidence, what they will do is to simply refuse to accept the election results on fabricated charges, and continue to exercise every single executive and congressional lever to prevent the recognition of the Democratic victors. Get ready for it. Absolute chaos.

comments.name: WhiskeyTangoFoxtrot

For what was expended on this tomfoolery over the last nearly two years, they could have used all that time, effort, and taxpayer dollars for something worthwhile - like healthcare. This would be funny if it wasn't so depressing...Russia could end the war at anytime, it's a war of choice and a war of aggression. Trump should be completely side-lined moving forward and should have nothing to do with giving Russia more cover.

comments.name: Sean
comments.body:
That the current scale of the healthcare crisis is not enough to warrant action for Congress is incredible to consider. 

I often wonder, what more do they want? What level of bankrupticies and avoidable deaths will it take? How many millions have to lose insurance they could barely use anyway? 

 How many families have to never form or stop after one child, like my wife and I are being forced to do? 

We are $12,000 in debt for having a child, with possibly more debt to come. And we have "great insurance". So good my wife will be dropped from the plan this year and go uninsured. The fingers crossed plan. 

If everything keeps going up, I will not be be able to afford my sons health insurance next year. Not while continuing to pay the mortgage. 

So where is this mythical breaking point where the system acknowledges this is enough suffering and acts? 

I'd love to know. 

I'd love to be able to have another kid one day. 

 I'd love to be able to move out of our tiny apartment. 

But maybe we all just got too greedy? Maybe I should be grateful I have a roof and shutup. 

I do hope United Healthcare, the US Senate, and every other elitist organization that benefits from this corrupt mess of health system is happy with themselves. 

I hope it was worth it.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: Sorry. So long as profit remains a lynch pin remains a large proportion of health care, and there are large numbers of people uninsured and unable to pay for their care, no amount of little reforms will shift the needle. Start by allowing buy in to public systems from certain groups. Over 55 and uninsured, buy into Medicare, just missed the Medicaid cut off- buy into Medicaid. When the level of uncompensated care goes down and for profit is regulated, overall costs will stabilize.

comments.name: P
comments.body: There seems to be a big push during this Medicare season to move folks into Advantage Plans which often fail and cancel you out. They are for profit. My D Plan with Aetna was canceled and I have never met the Deductible.  I will now start another Plan.  There are so few left to choose from.

comments.name: Wesley
comments.body: If an analysis of the US health care system doesn't end in universalizing our system to make sure every single person gets access then it isn't an analysis, it is rhetoric meant to protect this deeply broken system. We are the richest empire to ever exist, with endless money for war and subsidies, yet we have people dying in parks across the country because they happened to get sick. The milquetoast solutions in this article won't fix any of our problems and will do nothing more than allow this broken system to limp along into the future, plus there's a typo in the first sentence. The quality of these op-eds is seriously in decline.

comments.name: Will Tell
comments.body:
For years, I was told Obamacare would solve the problem. Some very smart people told me that it was all a ruse and that its true intent was to destroy the entire system, and then to clean it up, the Democrats could try to get universal healthcare through something like Medicare for all. It looks like they were right because Obamacare just made matters worse. So, at the very least, we can say that Democrats are liars and vile partisan hypocrites. But stating the obvious doesn't help the issue. No budget has yet been shown that could support universal Medicare. The cost isn't just trillions; it grows because when something is free, demand goes up, causing massive delays and hyper-demand with diminishing supply. 
Democrats will tell you that Europeans have universal healthcare. But we've already established that Democrats are lying schemers, and what they will never tell you unless you go there yourself and see is that European healthcare is a disaster. The wait lines are massive. It takes months to get a doctor's appointment. Most Europeans pay for private health insurance to supplement their so-called government healthcare. 
Democrats have this delusion that they can make it all free, and the government sets salaries for all doctors and nurses, etc., and that this will encourage all the bright students to flock to healthcare. Demand will skyrocket, and our supply of medical personnel will keep pace, because every doctor I know wants to work for the government.  It's a lie.

comments.name: SeaAlTell

If we want an overhaul of our healthcare system, then it's important to vote Blue today. 

If you have already voted, be sure to track your ballot to make sure it was accepted. Depending on your state you may only have until polls close today to address any problems or you may have several days. 

There is still time to phone bank or door knock today to help get out the vote. Volunteers are also needed to cure ballots. Let's do this!

Some stayed out of conviction but many stayed because their lives were built there and they were not particularly enchanted with the foreign Arab intervention into the conflict. Like the U.S., Israel needs to change course from a culture of conflict and hate to cooperative governance and equality among citizens.

comments.name: Blanche White
comments.body:
A two state solution is delusional.

Likewise, Arabs, due to the nature of the entire ME, should be Arab citizens in a Jewish State. The history of the Arab attacks against Israel going back to the beginning cannot be denied. 

There can be a parallel advisory board for Arab issues to make sure they are front and center in a Jewish controlled State. ...and I believe that Israel, discounting their most extreme faction, knows that having a healthy society for all residents means that Arab issues are important too.

Considering the nature of the Israeli State, its birth and its continuing need to make its security its most important mission, then that mission would be threatened by sharing its government with any group whose values are possibly in conflict with their's.

We have evidence all over the world as to why this is so. Yet there continues to be those who cannot believe that square pegs do not fit in round holes.

For now, I think the Arabs who have fought alongside Israelis, are happy to live in a well run and prosperous State.

Untill enough time passes to see if changes could be made   without a national security risk, then the Israeli State requires a Jewish government.

What an aptly named law. It’s no surprise that an insurer will try to avoid paying. It’s also no surprise that medical providers will try to enrich themselves by gaming the system . It’s no surprise that arbitrators are looking out for themselves by allowing ineligible cases into the system. 
That’s as American as apple pie.

comments.name: ABJ
comments.body: Greed and grift in the medical industry. Truly no surprise there. Can't say I'm sympathetic to either side. At the end of the day, it's the patient who always loses.

comments.name: Susan F
comments.body:
Arbitrators are REWARDED by how many cases they settle, and the insurers are saying the arbitrators are taking cases that should not go to arbitration. Then awarding fees anywhere from 40-100 pct higher than the insurer allows. 
Here's the smoking gun:
"Some (providers) who have built their businesses around the arbitration system and its high payouts have taken on debts to stay afloat."
I understand providers think they are underpaid, but a bunch of them are now abusing the arbitration system and WE ALL PAY via higher insurance premiums. That must have been a poorly written law. Do better.

comments.name: J M
comments.body: I'm not sure what and isn't fair but my strong but 87 year old husband had a cancer surgery at a major U med center in SoCal and a 3 day hospitalization.  The 135k bill was denied as not medically necessary. After two appeals 9k was paid . That's super low. Fast forward to a nationally known cancer center where he gets an $800 injection per discount card price but the treatment center charges Anthem just under 25K per shot every 3 wks. Anthem reimburses 6k something.  None of it makes sense.

comments.name: SloopJohnB
comments.body: Gaming the system is perfectly legal and even logical.  Arbitration is a zero sum game, literally.  One wins, one loses.  It encourages the two involved to put their best claim forward...if the arbitrator awards a very high MD claim, it's generally because the insure puts the claim at a ridiculously low level, not necessarily the level the insurance company considers fair and reasonable.  With the MD claim perhaps relatively high, the award goes to the MD because the insurer is unreasonable.

comments.name: SmylyMatt
comments.body:
Anthem CEO Gail Boudreaux' salary : $20, 471, 976

United CEO Brian Thompson 's salary : 1 Million, plus $341,884 in "Other" compensation 

Cigna CEO Brian Evanko's salary : $1,300,000

Aetna CEO Steve Nelson's salary : 11, 587, 110

Yet these insurance companies at the direction of the individuals listed above, refuse to pay medical arbitration awards . And of course, the Trump administration can't be bothered to compel them to pay,  because starting a war in Iran is far more important.

That's the the sick and inhumane  joke joke that is  the broken healthcare system in this country.

comments.name: ALEX

It’s got ridiculous and more dangerous and it needs to be stopped. 

None of this should be allowed in a country where the health of the population is supposed to be top priority.  

Instead a tiny handful of people are making billions at everyone else’s expense. The outcomes of this are absolutely unknown and likely carry more risk to humanity than anything else in history. 

The rogue AI agents that are being created are able to be pointed at targets daily human lives.  

The attack of good refrigeration in Europe is a perfect example of how this can proceed. It’s staggering what is coming. 

Now this madness outlined in this article.  It is absolutely insane.

comments.name: AG
comments.body: Unfortunately, what comes to mind is the horrific image captured of the Lear jet plane crash in Florida 2 days ago and the reported last communication-"We're out of time."  I can't honestly know that humanity is out of time but the emergency demands better Heads of Government to be in place to do all we can.

comments.name: AJC
comments.body: So they also run on diesel. I’m sure the farmers are thrilled to be competing for gas with Musk. We should make sure they know, because I’m sure they’ll be all for it then. Same with the truckers.

articles.title: Old, Polluting Jet Engines Are Being Scavenged to Power Data Centers
Five Takeaways From Democrats’ Midterm Blowout
articles.summary: Voters delivered a rebuke to President Trump, rebalancing power in Washington.

comments.name: Jim Strinka
comments.body: If we get a Democratic President in 28, do we have to go again through another incredibly series of painstaking negotiations towards a nuclear agreement with Iran ( if it's even possible ) ?  It took years to strike a deal, and weeks to tear it down.

comments.name: Carl Bowen
comments.body: Now that power is restored to the Democrats, how long until benefits are realized in our pocketbooks (as measured by net income to net expenses)?

comments.name: Mahatma Kane Jeeves
comments.body: Perhaps the best outcome of this election would be that Republicans no longer see the need to kiss Trump's ring.  The people have spoken, and they don't care who Trump says they should vote for.  Maybe this will create a path to a normal, center-right Republican Party of the Eisenhower/Nixon/Reagan/GHWB/GWB eras.  Many of us would love to return to a Republican Party without the grift, incompetence, personality disorders and craziness.

comments.name: Tilo K
comments.body:
"So much winning, you will get tired of winning".

Not today, Donny!!!

comments.name: Tilo K
comments.body:
Donny: "Had I been on the ballot, we would have won".

Gee, how delusional do you have to be to come up with this statement????

comments.name: Theodore Gazulis
comments.body: It seems clear that corruption played a large role, all across the spectrum. But the phrasing used in the article “… alleged  government corruption“ misses the mark (whether intentionally or not). I don’t think the corruption allegations are generalizable to the “government” - they’re squarely focused on President Trump, his family and other members of the administration. However those allegations play out over time, the electorate seems uncomfortable with the president generating more than $2 billion of incremental net worth over the last couple of years.

comments.name: D R Ryan
comments.body:
Yup.  It was us independents that did it.  17% turnaround. 

The more folks that leave the two broken parties, the better.

comments.name: Roger Floyd
comments.body:
I hope the Democrats focus on ending the Iran war, the tariffs and therefore helping with affordability. 

Endless hearings into Trump family corruption, while justified, will be a huge distraction. However, they should certainly impeach Hegseth for doing a shockingly nasty job of managing the armed forces.

comments.name: Dale Swift
comments.body: Mr. Ronan, I think I love you!!! My sentiments, exactly.

comments.name: Rick
comments.body:
We have an alarming lack of basic civics and history knowledge to overcome here.   

If we could help people see that the extent to which wealth and services are collected and redistributed is better seen as a matter of degrees and a matter of who gives and who gets, I think people would be very surprised by how misinformed they are about the true nature of "socialism" here in the US.  

We could get here without even requiring a 200-level course.

comments.name: Qev
comments.body: Anti-Woke ran into a buzzsaw, henceforth to be referred to as  Anti-WOAT (Worst Of All Time).

comments.name: John Q Public
comments.body: The wave of BROWN not BLUE spoke, and was HEARD.

comments.name: Keith Davis
comments.body: Why they rejected Trump? Let me see, I'm going to think real hard... Oh, that's right -- because he's a LIAR, a convicted felon, foul-mouthed person with no moral compass other than his own wallet. As for rejecting the Republican Party itself, the elected members of congress sat back and let it happen. That's why yesterday happened. Thanks be to God!

comments.name: Betsy
comments.body: I want a boring president. . . one who just does his job, honestly and who leads ALL the people.

articles.title: Americans on Why They Rejected Trump’s Republican Party
articles.summary: A G.O.P. voter in Kansas put it bluntly: “The Republican Party has lost its way.”

comments.name: Cork Patterson
comments.body: I find it interesting that maybe pushback against the abortion law and the deterioration of the education system may have played a key role here.  I for one just cannot understand how the criminalization of medical decisions should be tolerated anywhere.  Maybe this will eventually lead to rethinking this.  Please understand that I'm not all that pro-abortion.  Personally, when I heard the phrase right to life, I always sort of agreed with it, but would amend it to be 'right to a decent life'.  Until our government and social structures can guarantee that 'decent' element, they should allow pregnant women to make the decision whether they themselves can imagine and provide a decent and loving life for their child.

comments.name: Lara
comments.body: I am 30-something Texan whose first major election to vote in was in 2016, when I was a hopeful college student. The results of that election were a shock to the system. Like many, I since learned to expect disappointment on election nights. The results from last night are more than a dream come true. Today, for the first time in my adulthood, I can say I am proud to be a Texan. What an incredible thing to be part of.

comments.name: UV
comments.body: I'm in Austin, and I am stunned (and ecstatic) by the results. I was hoping Talarico would win, but wasn't expecting Texas's state government to flip to blue. Just had a discussion with a couple of people before the election. One said, "Texas will always be red." Boy was she wrong.

comments.name: S
comments.body:
• Can Texas truly turn purple or blue in a lasting way? Talarico is a completely unique talent and seems like the model for how to turn Texas blue. BUt as we all know, had the winds of laughably horrible opposition behind him, in addition to general fury at Trump. 
• From one the ground I suspect a mixture of affordability, humane immigration policy, and exasperation with wars, AI, and corruption to be some of the guiding forces contributing to this win in Texas especially. What can we expect Gina H to reasonably do in Texas with the shape of the courts and Texas house and Senate? What can we expect Talarico and his colleagues in congress to do with Trump still in office and the court firmly in conservative hands?

comments.name: David
comments.body: Let us not neglect the lieutenant governor fall, as well. Significant power in that position here. Good day for education in this state.

comments.name: M
comments.body: Two things especially struck me in all this, one is, can you imagine how much good, how many people could have been fed or gotten a doctor's visit with all that money that was spent in this election?  And two, the Republican who said you "don't give your enemy a beachhead.". That's the problem.  We're fellow Americans, not the enemy.  I really hope this election is a harbinger of better things to come, but this cannot be a one and done.  People have got to realize that they need to keep voting, keep working hard to make sure we can get on the right track.  It's going to take years to undo the damage, let alone prosper.

comments.name: SATXGuy
comments.body: Perhaps now Texas can achieve the greatness it has always proclaimed as it’s destiny: restore women’s health rights, restore public education, restore the state University system to its past glory, tame unbridled, ostentatious displays of wealth and power by limiting data centers or at a minimum constructing the infrastructure - both electric and water - necessary to sustain them. Texas has 31 million people drawn from every ethnicity race, religion, sexual orientation and political persuasion and for the first time in over 30 years that extraordinary diversity has a voice. All the oligarchs and all the Christian nationalist’s money proved to be for nothing; the legislature and the governor’s mansion they bought and paid for went up in smoke, proving that even Texans have a breaking point. Now it’s time for Elon to move to Florida.

comments.name: Jane
comments.body:
Stunned and overjoyed. So happy for Texans, our family and friends who live there in particular. Thank you voters! Feels like a return to civility and democracy, as aspirational as it is. 

Love the David and Goliath metaphor. However my immediate response is that Senator-elect Talarico is Americans’ sling shot. Texan voters beat Goliath. Democracy over privilege and wealth.

articles.title: ‘An Earthquake’: A Democratic Rout Stuns Texas
articles.byline: J. David Goodman and Lauren McGaughy
articles.summary: In a seismic shift that was once unthinkable, victories by James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa upended decades of statewide dominance in what had been the nation’s most populous conservative state.

comments.name: Arthur
comments.body:
I find the general public’s lack of awareness of who supplies the foods to most restaurants hilarious.

I remember moving to Dallas, and learning that everyone had a ‘favourite’ Tex-mex spot.

The first thing I noticed was that the menus are 90% identical to each other (menu planning at work, again.). If you pointed this out, the fan who brought you there would then insist that the was this place did it was absolutely unique and stood tall against everyone else’s offerings.

Almost invariably, when I eventually went to the men’s room, I would pass by the kitchen, and either through swinging doors, or strategically placed winds, see a kitchen or kitchen storage area stacked to the ceiling with Sysco premade contents, from rice, to beans, to salsas.

Such is the power of perception.

To be fair, one had to acknowledge that when many patrons developed their cultish like of the restaurant, it was smaller, and well before large suppliers like Sysco were on the scene, or had developed offerings for specific ethnic food specialties….

comments.name: LEM
comments.body:
Not sure where the efficiency is when I see three Sysco trucks on the same block each delivering one pallet to three different restaurants. Simultaneously.

All double parked blocking travel lanes, bike lanes, or crosswalks.

comments.name: ga
comments.body: It's gotten to the point where I can always tell if foods at a mom and pop are not house made.  We loved a creative seafood restaurant some miles away when it first opened and the next couple of years.  The last visit, the fries were definitely not up to par with the seafood.  We haven't been back.

comments.name: World’s Foremost Authority
comments.body: Private equity has played an important role in hollowing out the restaurant dining experience over the last 30 years. The expression I prefer is sucking the jelly out of the jelly donut, slowly at first, then suddenly. With the heavy application of technology enabled business models I no longer feel that I’m no longer going out to dinner but going out for business - theirs.

comments.name: New Senior
comments.body:
I leave for work very early in the morning and walk past a very popular company that has soft serve yogurt with an array of toppings. The line for buying a cup was around the corner in the summer. I hate waiting on lines and so have not sampled this allegedly amazing treat.
Most of the time I see a Sysco truck making a delivery of dozens of containers and suddenly wondered if the secret ingredient that makes the yogurt so popular is really a soft serve mix from Sysco?
Ouch - is this a case of getting the base ingredients and making a unique product, or is this a culinary case of The Emperor's New Clothes? I'll save my money and my time.

comments.name: Birding
comments.body: When I eat out I seek out Thai, West African, Korean, Indian, sea food, and Mexican restaurants run by local families. I depend on word-of-mouth for recommendations. I am lucky to live in Oregon where we have good places to eat. I find that restaurants with more than one location have little flavor or substance to their meals. Brand restaurants are uniformly poor quality. No, I don’t eat those donuts.

comments.name: jean Louis Lonne
comments.body: In France , and particularly the Parisien area there are Sysco like companies; the next step is doing away with the kitchen; replacing it with microwave ovens.  I can warn potential diners to review the menu carefully; if there's too much variety of the type that can be reheated; stay away. It will be the death of good food.  And what is so hard about peeling a potato?  Here in Portugal, many still do; some don't, I never eat twice in them.

comments.name: Mary Ann
comments.body: Whatever the merits/drawbacks may be, I was stopped dead at "dynamic pricing".  Congress should outlaw it, period.  Additionally, they need to rein in the burgeoning monopolistic behavior across all industries.

articles.title: Sysco Is Ruining American Restaurants. Or Saving Them.
articles.summary: Depending on whom you ask, the giant food distributor is flattening the way we eat, or helping small business owners survive. Maybe both are true?

comments.name: AKJersey
comments.body:
No, Democrats won because the price of gas is too high, and Trump got blamed.
The personal attributes of individual candidates was irrelevant.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:
One thing many a self-proclaimed “moderate” doesn’t seem to understand about what the GOP has become under Trump is that he will not ALLOW a conservative to be moderate within his party (… and it is “his,” conservatives, you willingly gave it to him).

When it comes to Trump you are in or you are out. There is no “middle” with him.

Did conservatives want reasonable border security? Tough. Trump won’t allow anything but atrocity.

Did conservatives want some moderate approach to Iran? Tough: Trump won’t allow anything but a quixotic mission of complete subjugation.

Did conservatives want some sane examination of spending. Tough. All Trump has to offer is Musk, DOGE, and his army of frat-boy kleptocrats.

Moderation is 100% anathema to everything MAGA and Trump stand for. He himself has made things binary, even within his own party. Your are either in or out.

comments.name: too old....
comments.body: There used to be a saying, same 'ole person, what can we do. Well Maine finally said.. out with the dirty dish water. It is a much newer environment in Maine today, than 30 yrs ago. As such, this election showed a new movement.

comments.name: Janet Wainwright
comments.body:
I am a staunch Democrat, but I once contributed to Susan Collins many,  years ago. She has disappointed time and time again. Her support of most of Mr Trump's nominees and policies were not in keeping with her claims to be a maverick. The only true Republican maverick in the senate is Lisa Murkowski. She is better than faux democrat, John Fetterman.

May the blue wave bring relief to the people and hold the the corrupt Republicans accountable.

comments.name: Carl
comments.body: As described "a giant of the senate" - no, she was a mere caricature of herself.  Really a no-principle wimpy do-nothing.  Its good that she's out.

comments.name: TCW
comments.body: Collins' hand-wringing, followed by immediate capitulation to Trump will not be missed

comments.name: Ray
comments.body: I was always a Susan Collins supporter until she confirmed Kavanaugh who overturned Roe V Wade and the eccentric RFK. So sad. She lost her courage.

comments.name: Annie
comments.body: It's about time!

articles.title: Maine Voters Finally Saw Through Susan Collins
articles.summary: One of the greatest survivors in U.S. politics finally falls.

comments.name: Rachel
comments.body:
Wonderful to read such good news! Thank you!
As others have said, where can we donate to support this effort? 
And what else can people improve to benefit mothers and children?

comments.name: Upperclaremont
comments.body: What a great tool. Due to post part haemorrhage I had an Hgb of 5.5 (!), the nurse on duty at night just changed the linen.  (Germany, 1990). It took me many years to get it to 12 again. Where can I donate?

comments.name: kim
comments.body:
“The drape is not an A.I. thing — it’s the absolute opposite: It’s a simple, simple, intervention that can solve our problems,” she said.”

Between this and the blue wave, I'll have my first good night's sleep in two years.

comments.name: Jaya
comments.body:
Great news to wake up to! Simple solution for a deadly problem. Kudos to whoever developed this brilliant device! 

Did a bit of quick research and it seems it is called the E-MOTIVE bundle developed in 2002 by “the KLE JNMC Women’s and Children's Health Research Unit in Belgaum, India, in collaboration with the University of Missouri-Kansas City and the University of Illinois at Chicago”. But this is only mentioned on Instagram. Couldn’t find any papers. 

The WHO reported on it in 2023 after the results of a “trial of a set of interventions to manage postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) published in the New England Journal of Medicine, found a 60% reduction in heavy bleeding.”

Women are benefiting from this bundle of interventions and it is heartening to hear that Nigeria is producing it for nationwide distribution.

comments.name: Audrey
comments.body: What a brilliantly simple, effective, low-tech idea. I bet it saves more lives than AI and all its energy sucking mega data centres ever will.

comments.name: Girl Bird
comments.body: There’s no joy here. Most of these women are hidden in Islamic clothing and forced to give birth to endless children. Male birth control is desperately needed. A mother or newborn may survive but only to die later of another horrible disease. We cannot support societies and religions where impregnation is involuntary. I thought we learned that here.

comments.name: Cs
comments.body: Keeping this article in my back pocket for when I need a pick me up. More reporting resources please to Africa please!

comments.name: John
comments.body: Having delivered hundreds of babies over my years as a physician, mostly in rural Canada, this is the best news for expecting women around the world in these challenging times, as increasingly, indigent women and their families are faced with the challenges of bringing a child safely into this world in places lacking the most basic services. This proves that, with trained staff and bundled resources ready to support safe obstetrical care, we can start to bring back the obstetrical services that have been lost to many rural places. It is so wonderful that this has come out of research in Africa, in part due the support of the Gates Foundation, despite the politicization and withdrawal of humanitarian support by the US government. I expect that this will, ironically, emerge into the protocols of every delivery room in America very shortly, as I’m sure it will in Canada. Congratulations to the wonderful team that developed this! You deserve a Nobel Prize for your scientific achievement, which has the potential to profoundly reduce maternal mortality around the world, yet costs just pennies. Simply brilliant!

articles.title: An 80-Cent Plastic Pouch Is Saving Thousands of Women From Dying in Childbirth
articles.summary: The maternal drape, as it is called, is helping to solve one of the world’s most intractable health problems.

comments.name: Jacob Montgomery
comments.body: Give credit to Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani. Ossoff's rhetoric originated with them. Would Ossoff hold the Trump administration accountable or play nice? Would he end our disastrous closeness with Israel, or not? He talks the talk but we question whether he will walk like Sanders and Mamdani have.

comments.name: Mike Cyr
comments.body: YOU are literally joking, right?  Roy Cooper not only won by a greater margin he led a political earthquake - a virtual bloodbath - in North Carolina with almost no political precedent.  Cooper gutted the GOP's control of the State of North Carolina - he was like Godzilla wrecking the gerrymandering nirvana the GOP thought it had built there.  The only person you should be writing about is Roy Cooper.

comments.name: Who’s trying to prevent him from running
comments.body:
Ossoff is a contender for 2028, but there’s no one hiring influencers and podcasters to taint male politicians like him in an effort to dissuade his run for presidency. But there are plenty doing that to dissuade AOC from running. 

Republicans billionaires are threatened by AOC, but not so much by Ossoff. This should give every voter a clue as to who will be looking out for their interests and the interests of their children (ie the future).

Some media outlets have a habit of looking out for rich people’s interests because they choose to hire a lot of people who come from that background. Look out for your interests and your family’s interests by seriously considering the one person who isn’t rich, didn’t grow up rich, doesn’t have a desire to become rich, and who isn’t backed by special interest billionaires. That person is AOC.

Hillary and Kamala got more anti-Trump votes than pro votes. AOC will get more AOC votes. Republicans voted for Trump because they wanted radical change. Trump didn’t deliver. He made fake promises. AOC will deliver. 100% guaranteed.

comments.name: Michelangeles
comments.body: Voters were offered, and chose, a smart and decent man to represent them. Sounds simple but not something we've seen much of recently. Let's hope this is the dawn of a new day. Well done team Ossoff.

comments.name: DM
comments.body:
Not suddenly, he has been right in front of you.

But, let’s let him do the work of being a Senator; that is whatever’s elected to this night!

comments.name: JB
comments.body: I've been posting #Ossoff2028 for two years!

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: Sorry, but no. We cannot have another Democratic president who is loyal to Our Closest Ally above all else. It is time to cut all ties, and Ossoff won't do that.

comments.name: Sally
comments.body: Happy to see Ossoff glide to victory!! I would like to see a proper Presidential primary on the Democrotic side and I hope Senator Ossoff puts his name in the ring

articles.title: Jon Ossoff Suddenly Looks Even More Presidential
articles.summary: Fighting corruption, the theme in his race, could work for Democrats in 2028.

comments.name: Sarah Bradshaw
comments.body: Friends and family thought I had some sort of crystal ball but due to MS NOW's excellent and extended coverage of 3-time Trump voters, I knew this was coming. I really do have to give thanks to their entire team of correspondents and anchors who have kept hope alive, stuck with decency and provided a information North Star when so much was being lost. To be honest, I leave it on 24/7 but as a result, I am better informed on DC and national political issues than 95% of my peers.

comments.name: Jeff P.
comments.body:
It's absolutely hilarious that the cable news network with the highest ratings keeps musing about "mainstream media." How not self-aware can you possibly be?

NBC and ABC seemed to be a little more constrained in their coverage, with more analysis than celebration, but not by much. Regardless, the engagement for a midterm was pretty extraordinary. Maybe people will start paying attention.

comments.name: Eva Marie
comments.body: I couldn't help myself and turned on Fox to see how it was covering the wipeout. A pundit said with confidence and certainty that Trump's pros had outweighed his cons, so there could be only one explanation: Socialism. So there you have it. After having a good laugh I returned to networks living in the real world.

comments.name: Renee
comments.body:
The relief is palpable. Now there needs to be balance in rectifying what can be rectified, moving forward, and punishing the most egregious ethical assaults made to the country. 

Too much time spent on punishment will doom long-term Democratic gains but complete inattention will embolden future attempts for politicians to enrich themselves.

comments.name: Lisa C.
comments.body: I am giddy about the results. It is a flash of hope. The Democrats need to quickly (very quickly) address the sins of Trump and the GOP (e.g., ACA, Iran war, ICE, overspending, incapable members of the administration, corruption, vanity projects, etc.). Presented as separate bills, they will be better able to sell each to the public and focus potential vetoes on Trump. They should do this with the same vigor they ran on. While all of this is happening, investigate the holy heck out of this administration and their enablers.

comments.name: Keith
comments.body: I hope the Democrats seek to legislate change that will stand up to partisan criticism, for example banning stock trading, tighter ethics rules and campaign finance reform.  Holding ICE accountable for its brutality would only get blowback from the most conservative voters as well.  Reversing some of the worst parts of HR 1 might take longer and would likely face a veto.  Focus on kitchen table items and basic decency!

comments.name: Tammy
comments.body: Democrats must act swiftly to hold Trump and the Republican Party accountable for their actions. A prompt response is necessary. However, Democrats should also reconsider their positions on certain divisive issues (like boys in girls' sports) and maintain strong border policies. We cannot afford a repeat of past mistakes. If Democrats fail to adapt and learn, Republicans are likely to regain power—and recent history has shown what they are willing to do to destroy ou r country and have our people live in fear.

comments.name: Kat Dog
comments.body: I'm very happy about the election results, but it's just going to be more of the same. The Democrats will spend their time in power trying to clean up the mess Republicans have made, while the Repubs yell "tax and spend Democrats" and just generally try to gum up the works. Voters will get tired yet again of the dysfunction and will vote against the party in power. This is no way to run a nation.

articles.title: Candy and Smiles on MS NOW, and Some Regrets on Fox News
articles.byline: Michael M. Grynbaum and John Koblin
articles.summary: On TV, the outcome of the midterm elections became clear early on. Pundits celebrated and grieved by turns.

comments.name: Kristine
comments.body: This is hilarious!  Maybe it would have been better to just invest in our public schools, allowing the experts to develop comprehensive programs that serve all children with a high quality education.  Instead we have an idiot leading the department of education (not leading exactly, destroying is more accurate) and a president that doesn't give a rip about education because he clearly failed at learning anything in school.

comments.name: dan
comments.body:
The whole reason school choice is so fraught is because public education is so abysmal. But we democrats won't go there because that would mean taking on Teachers' Unions. 
I went to public school. I will fill out a thousand forms and pay thousands of dollars to spare my children that fate

comments.name: hen3ry
comments.body:
This reminds of the gag routine Garrison Keillor did on a phone menu during "A Prairie Home Companion".  The audience couldn't stop laughing even though, when we're stuck in one of them, it's anything but funny.

I don't see why parents need to experience this sort of frustration over a public school selection.  Then again, this frustration is part and parcel of American life as a whole.  Rather than a few well thought out choices, we're offered too many choices with most being inappropriate, the best ones being too expensive, and we're always wondering how much we're being cheated.

Perhaps it's really an early lesson to children, via their parents, of how inept this country has become at meeting real needs such as decent school choices without anguish.

articles.title: Dear American Parent: You’re Welcome!
articles.summary: Hey, no one said having all this freedom was going to be easy. Or survivable.

comments.name: Matt Andrews
comments.body:
Stopping Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons was a valid reason for war. They had enriched uranium to levels that have no civilian use. No nation has ever enriched uranium to that degree and NOT developed a bomb. I have no idea why readers - and reporters - at the NYT continuously downplay or glaze over this fact. 

It was imperative to stop them before. And it's imperative to stop them now.

comments.name: Jk
comments.body:
The present extremist government of Iran, were it to achieve weapons grade nuclear capability, would make their first targets Israel and then America?

Maybe Israel is right?

comments.name: John H.
comments.body:
It's only natural that Iran would want a nuclear missile at its disposal,  a weapon that would ward off unprovoked attacks on its population by Israel and the U.S. 
A nuclear-armed Israel is, in my mind, the greatest threat to stability in the region. If Iran had a nuclear bomb, Israel would likely give up its habit of bombing its neighbors.

comments.name: dean ford
comments.body: No nation has the right to tell another nation they can not have nuclear weapons unless no nation has nuclear weapons. We can not ignore that moral dilemma even though all the nations who have nuclear weapons will try.  I got an idea..Let's make peace with Iran. Real peace

comments.name: Blackray
comments.body:
Saddam Hussein in Iraq, Gaddafi in Libya and the Ukrainian leadership all gave up their WMD's and look what happened to them. Iran negotiated deals and was stabbed in the back. Meanwhile North Korea is safe and sound.

The lesson from this is that if you want to deter a Western attack, develop WMD's.

comments.name: Kate
comments.body:
Ironic how Israel and the US may achieve through their unprovoked war exactly the outcome they ostensibly launched the war to avoid.

Iran still has a fatwa against developing a nuclear weapon. Fatwas are serious. Again, a bit ironic how the same folks who decry Iran as religious fanatics can't believe that a declaration that has the full force of that religion behind it might actually be for real. I'm not sure whether the fatwa can be canceled--I'm no expert on Iranian religion. But unless something changes, it seems unlikely that they will actually produce a nuclear weapon, although they might come as close as possible without exactly producing one.

While I think nuclear proliferation is always dangerous, I can't blame Iran for wanting to have nuclear weapons or at least the capacity to build them. Dating back to the 1953 CIA coup that toppled Iran's secular democracy, the US has proven itself to be both aggressive and duplicitous. Iranians have not forgotten 1953. They have every reason to fear and no reason to trust the US. The Trump administration deepened that mistrust by attacking  Iran twice while negotiations were underway. The US and Israel seem to be doing everything possible to convince Iran that they need nuclear weapons.

comments.name: abraham quisling
comments.body: Afghanistan, Libya, venezuela, Iraq, iran. for sure iran needs nuclear missiles. every country that the US doesn’t like needs nuclear missiles. Canada needs nuclear missiles. Greenland needs nuclear missiles.

comments.name: Art
comments.body: Frankly it's rather shocking they wouldn't have come to this conclusion way back when trump "tore up" the Obama-era agreement some years ago.

articles.title: Facing Return to War, More Iranians Want a Nuclear Missile
articles.summary: Some Iranian clerics and officials argue the country must rebuild deterrence by dropping its longstanding pledge not to build a nuclear bomb.

comments.name: Laura From Michigan
comments.body: Gee, if only Elon Musk, the former trillionaire and still richest person on the  planet, would use his obscenely vast amount of personal wealth for good (e.g.  health care for all, scientific research to eradicate childhood disease, funding public education in underfunded urban and rural areas, the list goes on...), think of the world we could live in!  But instead, this is a man who puts his money toward throwing elections in his favor so he doesn't have to pay taxes.  SMH.

comments.name: John
comments.body: It seems like his political spending was a much larger percentage of his liquid capital (up to 50%), which is the relevant statistic, not his paper wealth based on stock shares and options.

comments.name: MC
comments.body:
Now we will have the revenge of the out of control billionaires.  

Maybe when these tech bros who own governments shut down infrastructures, utilities and the Internet doesn't work with satellites going dark because Musk is upset, people will understand the threat the man poses.

comments.name: Stephen

I'm fascinated by his campaign - in my opinion he could have moderated his position on Israel ever so slightly and won by more, but he stuck to his principles even when it hurt him. I agree with the author - he's a great political talent, and I'm glad there's a place for him in my Democratic party - I just hope that his view of the Israel-Palestinian conflict doesn't become the dominant one in the party.

comments.name: Andrew
comments.body:
A quick tour of X right now shows an enormously gratifying amount of "cope" coming from the MAGA-sphere, and concurrently and unsurprisingly, the NYTimes centrists are here  to engage in their own form of "cope", desperate to combat the obvious lesson to be learned for the Democrats.  Across the country, voters sent a resoundingly clear message that a platform of left-leaning economic populism can win everywhere.

This election is without a doubt a complete rebuke of Trump and the first two years of his second term. But let's not forget that Democrats throughout those two years had also been overwhelmingly unpopular, even in the midst of such executive incompetence. If they return to a politics of middling centrism, confidently complacent with their electoral accomplishments, they will fritter their political capital and invite the resumption of a reassembled Republican machine, one that has no qualms about embracing populism as the antidote to milquetoast corporate moderation. 

The message can't be clearer. Get money out of politics, money in your pocket, Medicare for All. Cope all you want, but the answer to the future needs to be decisive, ambitious, and transformative. Moderates gave birth to both of Trump's presidencies; it's time to put them in their place.

It was closer than it needed to be, specifically because El-Sayed is Muslim with an Arabic name (which you cite matters to 38%).  I'm relieved his gifts overcame that handicap.
But the political lesson here is that McMorrow would have won easily, and with her strength she would have dragged a few more Congressional candidates over the finish line.
And in the Senate, you need 50+1 votes to pass a bill.  Whatever El-Sayed's gifts, his vote and McMorrow's vote would each count as 1 Democratic vote on a bill.
McMorrow was pushed out by a nefarious lie; this is common in politics.  You influence primaries to saddle your opponent with the least effective nominee.  MAGA champagne corks popped when McMorrow was sunk.
If the lesson you take is that it's best to nominate the riskiest candidate who your opponents think will lose, that's not a winning formula.

comments.name: Bethynyc
comments.body:
After I moved away from NYC and would return for visits, I would put out the call in a friends only post on social media. usually people who I had met in person before. 

If someone offered, I would accept, and we would sort out where to meet, how I could get back and forth, and where I would sleep. etc. I strived to be a good guest and not interfere with my friends' day to day routine.  

However, once I got to a certain age, sleeping on other people's couches wasn't fun any more. Now I stay in a hotel and still meet up with friends for dinner or museuming.

I can’t believe that this is a question.  Of course family members should always be welcome.
And friends, even friends of friends, should be welcome if it’s feasible for the hosts.  This is fundamental in Judaism.

In college I worked with a nice girl, we were friendly but not really friends. We never interacted outside of work, where we had different schedules, so we probably spent 3 hours together total over 4 years.

I moved to Manhattan after graduation and all of a sudden her calls began, pretty incessantly,  for a place to stay while she was doing auditions. I have no idea how she got my number, but I've since discovered she had a list of people she called.

Her request irritated me so much; to come out of the woodwork when you all of a sudden want something? No.

But I don't see anything wrong with fishing for an invitation, e.g., "I'll be in [your city] next week and I'm looking for an inexpensive place to stay a couple nights. Any ideas?" That gives the person a choice to either offer hospitality or avoid an awkward refusal.

comments.name: Měng quān

Part of the issue is that we have dumbed down the mean of the word friend to be basically on par with acquaintance.   I have friends and many of us we stay at each others place. They live in Paris, Croatia, Athens Greece, Hong Kong, Bangkok.  We became friends back in college and early work careers, we crashed at each others apartments when we were between places.  We babysat each other's kids, cooked meals for the funerals of the others parents, get invited to holiday dinner with the family if we happen to be in town.  If any of us showed up in the city where the other lived we wouldn't have to ask we'd be offered a place to stay and a home cooked meal.  That's what friend do.

I have only a few friends, but lots of acquaintances.

The hypocrisy of the centrist, corporate, do-nothing faction of the Democrats is absolutely astounding. After years of “Vote Blue No Matter Who” scolding over Hillary Clinton’s pathetic presidential campaign, they withheld support for El-Sayed, tarred him as an antisemite and jihadist, and issued gleeful predictions about his inability to win. articles.title: 8 States. 8 Democratic Wins. This Is Seismic.

comments.name: Karl
comments.body:
The NY Times headline "Jeffries in Line to be Speaker" is a  truism. Sure, he is in line, but let's not anoint him just yet. I'd like to see others in line too. The same goes for Schumer. 

Both men lead with milquetoast caution. That reflex for political safety over boldness will not meet this historic moment.

I -- and perhaps most Democrats -- would like to see a competitive leadership race for both House and Senate. Make them fight for the job and lay out their priorities. The country demands change, and traditional cautious politics puts protecting incumbency ahead of the hardscrabble debate needed to forge a new consensus.  

This moment requires imagination and no little passion to connect policy with the needs of struggling workers and families. This means not just confronting Trump (which is necessary) but setting the stage for 2028. Put popular bills on the floor for votes. Dare the Republicans to vote against them. Dare Trump to veto them. Then campaign on them in 2028.

Most of all, do not cater unduly to the donor class. This election was a victory of the people over the donors. Dark money actually worked against many incumbents this year.

Schumer and Jeffries may be the right tag team for the next Congress, but I'm not convinced. Most folks commenting here likewise seem unconvinced. That's not a good sign. 

Let the process for selecting the next leader be a rigorous one to ensure they have the seal of legitimacy. The people deserve no less.

comments.name: jb
comments.body: At a time of stunning success, you can count on democrats to complain. We can hardly find a word of praise and gladness before we wave our arms and demand that we get our way. Too centrist, too extreme, too quiet, too loud. Not the leader I want!! And the quarrels go on. The right’s unity has allowed its horrid successes. And our refusal to unite has been the single greatest weakness on the left. Any progress we make is in spite of it, not because of it. Let’s go forward anyway. We must.

comments.name: Nanci Dee
comments.body: Let's be clear...Democrats didn't get a mandate...this was a repudiation of Trump and MAGA. And, an opportunity to see if we can deliver on what every winning candidate promised...deal with affordability and corruption.  If we don't,  these swing voters will feel betrayed and stay home or vote for the better GOP candidates that will be delivered in '28.

comments.name: ADubs
comments.body:
This move throws water on my enthusiasm as it is an early sign that Dems have learned little about the dangers of prioritizing making history over making good policy. Hakeem Jeffries has show he does not possess the mettle to be an effective speaker.

Dems should be meticulously organized, ready on Day 1 to offer a raft of legislation aimed at helping the people who just put them in office. Force the GOP to show their hand in voting against everything, put Trump onstage vetoing everything. This is how to take control of the narrative, not by feel-good measures that please the voters for a few days but leave them seething two years from now when the presidency and SCOTUS are on the line.

comments.name: Alex
comments.body: It's disappointing to see same-old same-old starting to form already. Maybe 2028's nominee will knock some sense into them. For now, as others have said online, now that Democrats have won big, it's time to focus on our top priority: losing. Despite decades of "do-nothing Dems" as the go-to pejorative, the party seem determined to treat even the most overwhelming of Republican rebukes as a sign to continue business as usual. Leadership, please, bring POSITIVE CHANGE with your power. Voters have been demanding it for a decade, and they will spend every election running away from the incumbent until they receive it.

Let's face it, Middle East politics stands to create unresolvable division among Democrats and create opportunities for Republicans to claw back.

comments.name: Newbie
comments.body: I’m in my 40s and have never in my lifetime been more proud to be a Texan.  I finally feel hopeful that we can course-correct all of the damage that the Republican dominance in leadership in Texas has created over the last several decades.  Change in leadership is long overdue.  Congratulations, my fellow Texans!

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
In June 2023, the Texas Education Agency assumed control of Houston Independent School District, and the new superintendent immediately began closing libraries. As of October 2026, at least 194 HISD campuses no longer have functioning libraries. Around 130 campuses had zero book checkouts in the first two months of this school year. Most of these schools are in high-poverty areas, where students have few, if any, reading resources at home.
Nationally, Texas ranks:
•	4th-Grade Math: Ranked 8th nationally (an improvement from 14th in 2022).
•	4th-Grade Reading: Ranked 37th nationally (down four places).
•	8th-Grade Math: Ranked 34th nationally (a decline from previous years).
•	8th-Grade Reading: Ranked 44th nationally (down three places).
Hinojosa strongly opposes state-funded private school vouchers and state takeovers of local school districts. She ran on a platform to end the voucher program, audit vendor contracts, and redirect those funds to increase teacher salaries and lower class sizes significantly. She also intends to replace Education Commissioner Mike Morath, and she reiterated that promise last night.
Parents in school districts that the state has taken over, those who are facing takeover, and all others who believe in ensuring educational outcomes for all Texas students saw a candidate who understands Texas can and should do better.

Incredible outcome. The most meaningful win of the night. 

Abbott wasn't a cartoonish freak like Paxton, he was an entrenched establishment Republican with a tremendous base. This was never going to be an easy race. 

It is a rare day indeed that I am proud of my state's voters. It's a good feeling; hoping for more of it.

Hinojosa listened to her constituents’ concerns over data centers (legitimate concerns over data centers using enormous amounts of electricity and water, causing noise and air pollution and driving down property values) and the fact that Abbot received $20 million from data center-related donors over the course of his political career. 

Hinojosa put so much pressure on Abbott that he  issued a temporary pause and regulatory crackdown on new data center developments to protect the state's power grid, water resources, and residential electricity bills (most likely to be reversed once he was re-elected). 

Hinojosa also demanded that Abbot release the over 1,000 pages unredacted of emails between himself and Elon Musk (with Musk's massive data center and AI infrastructure plans for Texas). Trump said those who opposed data center “want to end up being backwards and poor”. 

Texas residents voted for the politicians (including James Talarico) who insisted that Texas was not for sale.

Will Medicare/Medicaid approve these drugs as first line therapies for all, or will insurers and PBMs make them unavailable to certain classes of individuals? Vertex has used roughly 50 AI companies to comb through its data set of 10,000 drug compounds, Leiden said. Not one managed to generate a working drug.

Putin for his insatiable greed and hunger for power and legacy and his coldbloodedness, to the lives of his own people let alone Ukraine's.

comments.name: jeansch
comments.body: There is a dominant theme in Putin's war on Ukraine. Putin leverages Soviet nostalgia—such as WWII victory cults, narratives of strength. Putin views the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union as a profound "catastrophe" primarily because it fragmented what he considers historic Russian lands and diminished Moscow's buffer against Western institutions like NATO. His own personality disorder including malignant narcism, grandiose self image, low empathy, and psychopathic tendencies much the traits of autocratic leaders is why he invaded Ukraine.

That irony is not lost on me. I applaud this author for not blindly following the conventional wisdom about this war, which affects us all, even if he runs with his subject matter a little too far.

“If a political party does not have its foundation in the determination to advance a cause that is right and that is moral, then it is not a political party; it is merely a conspiracy to seize power.” 

– President Dwight D. Eisenhower (1890–1969)

(Remarks at Fourth Annual Republican Women's National Conference, 6 March 1956.)

comments.name: Rob H
comments.body:
This almost feels disrespectful to Cooper's strength as a candidate. North Carolinians are not voting for Roy Cooper because he is boring and safe, and I don't think he would have lost against a more "charismatic" Republican candidate. He's someone it seems people are actually happy to be voting for because of his candidate quality.

Roy Cooper represented North Carolina excellently as a governor, and had positive approval throughout his entire time in elected office. His stances on the hot-button issues are both well-established and, based on polling, agreeable to the majority of North Carolinians. He has shown high levels of competency and has strong character - people know he's good at his job. I think a lot of people trust Cooper to actually accomplish what he's running on, and the issue of affordability he's running on resonates deeply with North Carolinians.

I can't speak for everyone, but to me, Roy Cooper campaigning on "Making Stuff Cost Less" points to how things are rough enough currently that people are struggling to afford their basic necessities. Bringing down your bills is only a good slogan if the price of your bills have become worryingly high. The price of food/gas/rent/electricity and concerns about making ends meet come up regularly in conversation when having small talk here. Roy Cooper recognizes that before we can have fancy campaign slogans or argue about social issues, we need to make sure that people can afford to eat and keep the power running.

comments.name: Susan

comments.name: Opinioned!

Time to have some class and decorum where and when they matter.

Which is everywhere and always.

Time to replace all Republicans.

comments.name: Witheld
comments.body:
Roy Cooper's success is mistifying to me, as a former North Carolinian. When I lived there I was a tipped employee and nearly everyone I knew was in the restaurant/ bar industry. 

COVID happened, we reopened, and then came the curfews, which did what they were supposed to do and made people decide it wasn't worth it to go out. So those of us who were relying on people going out for our income sat around and starved. NC wage for tipped employees is still $2.13/hr. Roy Cooper let us go back to work so the state wouldn't have to pay us unemployment, then made it impossible for us to make a living. 

It's darkly funny to me that he's running on affordability now. How will he execute affordability? By reducing minimum wage? Reducing property taxes for landlords? Cutting social security or medicaid? After what he did to my industry for the greater good, I don't trust him.

Lowering electric bills seems a pretty modest goal for a newly elected senator--doesn't it?

We're choking on pollution and climate change. Homelessness, the national debt, dictatorship by a demented thug, ill-advised attacks on other countries, Artificial Intelligence potentially eliminating millions of jobs, ever-worsening income and wealth inequality, ICE shooting innocent Americans in the streets, immigrant scapegoating, data centers threatne or already plague us.

And the election turned on electric bills? And on Roy Cooper's calm, reassuring public face?

Nothing against Roy Cooper--he seems like a good guy, best you can tell.

But if this is really what motivated voters (do you have any data that support your claim?), we're in even bigger trouble than Donald Trump's presidency screams.

comments.body:
Nice job, CVS, after gobbling up nearly every small owner-operated pharmacy everywhere I’ve ever lived, where the pharmacist formerly lived in the neighborhood and knew the street you and your family lived on, knew the chronic maladies of your grandparents, and whose kids you went to school with. 

Of course, they did have an impressive array of nail polishes. 

There’s a shuttered mega-CVS store not far from me which has been vacant for two or three years - an empty storefront with a ‘commercial space for rent’ sign pasted in the papered-over plate glass window.

comments.name: lori
comments.body:
My last two Rx refills were either delayed by CVS, or CVS could not get the drug at all. I went to my grocery store pharmacy and they had it immediately - no problem. This is for Progesterone, not some rare medication for a rare disease - Progesterone.

The other drug was a thyroid med, that I had to build two pills to get to the prescribed dosage, even though the manufacturer makes a pill in the proper dosage - so two copays ($30/ea) instead of one.

If the initial consolidation of the CVS companies was supposed to make things easier and less expensive for the public, quite frankly, I did not see it. They own every step of the distribution chain, and they can't get common drugs?

Something is definitely wrong here. I hope this change helps, but I somehow doubt it.

comments.name: Mike
comments.body:
I’ve been talking the drug Diltiazemfor a couple of years.  Pills are 180 mg, one a day.  My insurance company charges $24 for a 3-month supply.

During a recent hospital stay one of the doctors put in a refill for the same drug, but 90 mg TWICE a day.

When I went to the pharmacy to pick it up, it was $102 for a 1-month supply.  When I complained, the pharmacy said to contact my insurance company.

The explanation I got was the 180 mg version is considered a “Tier 2” drug, and 90 mg is considered “Tier 4.”  Huh?  Same drug, same daily dosage, at $8 vs $102 per month?

Our entire healthcare system is infuriating.

comments.name: ARL
comments.body:
'no contact' -- since you have no remorse for your action of mouthing off inappropriately, you should either get into counseling and, if it was during an episode of substance abuse, into rehab.  A mom of four is also a wife, and those five jobs alone mean she is not available to be your woodpile or your post-op nurse.  

If you haven't had the surgery, you need to talk to the social worker at the surgeon's office - often there is a post-op nurse that will travel to your home and do the skilled nursing needed in the period before you are able to take a ride and get in to the office. And of course you can make some meals in advance.

comments.name: Dr. MJ
comments.body:
Re no contact with Mom.  How old are the kids?  Teenagers?  You and Dad are on your own for two weeks while I take care of grandma.  Young kids?  Either we all go and stay with Grandma, or she comes and stays with us.  Can’t swing it?  Be up front so Mom can arrange 2 weeks at a rehab center or hire outside help to come in daily.  Most hospitals and outpatient centers won’t do an elective surgery if someone is not available to stay with the pt for a minimum of 24hrs.

Agree wholeheartedly with the answers to the other three.

comments.name: Jo
comments.body:
Jewelry:  Lying is just a burden on yourself that you have to maintain.    Better to come clean, on such a relatively low-stakes topic.    She might be stung and upset, and you’ll have to accept those consequences.    You can also offer to have the pieces remade custom to replicate the originals as an act of contrition, if it would make her feel better.

My mom gave me her defunct diamond solitaire engagement ring from my dad as one of my first real pieces of jewelry.   She was on board when I asked if I could reset it into more of a fashion ring.   I kept the empty solitaire setting for years, and then had the diamond reset back into it for nostalgia’s sake.   Once the jeweler reset, cleaned and polished the ring it was just dazzling.

comments.name: ms
comments.body:
Daughter makes a commitment to take care of Mom for two weeks post-surgery.  But she either has or makes plans to be away for part of those two weeks.

Daughter made a commitment that she didn't have to make.  Something as serious as surgery isn't something that it's easy to find post-care for.  And Daughter doesn't appear to have given any thought to how Mom should fill the gap.  Backing out on a social engagement isn't good etiquette, but this is a little more serious.

Why is Mom taking full responsibility for getting upset when Daughter puts her in a difficult situation by not honoring her commitment?

comments.name: anonymouse
comments.body:
Mother: you're both under a lot of stress with your surgery and her four kids. Go ahead and "work on yourself" to put her at ease and show that you understand her stress. Hopefully she will come around and understand yours.

Friend: When you sell a home, there is all sorts of documentation that you have to disclose. It's best for your friend to not seek out info that hasn't been disclosed to him so he can be honest. When I sold my place, I had to disclose if there were any bees nearby but I don't remember any need to disclose nearby construction. 

Daughter: Do you really think she would mind you remaking the jewelry? Seems petty. Try wearing the new pieces and see if she even notices.

comments.name: NSAID
comments.body: Be willing to apologize and own your mistakes of the past.  There is nothing more important than that- but it has to come from the heart, not be performative.... your daughter will know the difference.  I put the ball squarely in my parents court and neither owned their mistakes of our shared past.  My dad has passed & my mom is in her 80's.  I maintained our relationship but that relationship was/is permanently compromised.  While it is a shame & a loss (which I have processed), I accept that and accept that they just weren't capable of more.  It is what it is, it was painful getting to where I am now, I am at peace with myself for having tried (& glad I did), and life goes on.  My relationship with my children are much stronger from what I learned from this experience.

comments.name: Jason Smith
comments.body: When you make your exit, you use one of the most severe and impactful punishments possible and blow apart a family. Since this columnist seems to justify that there is a place for this in the general arsenal of maintaining mental health as opposed to reserving this for only the most severe situations, I would advise the parent to act in kind. Full no-contact. Full dis-inheritance. You want this? Then let's ensure you are accountable to it.

comments.name: Kalidan
comments.body:
MOTHER: If your daughter is irrational, therapy will not help.  If your daughter is rational, there are likely some clear reasons (linked to you) that are causing the problem, and your daughter does not want the burden of arguing with you.  I would hypothesize that there is deep hurt your daughter believed you caused and the recent argument was the straw that broke the back.

I understand you are grieving, but so is your daughter.  No one can predict who or when will come around, and what will happen as a result.  Accept the situation and move on.
