He did kill it in the rural areas of NYS, though. If the results are accurate, only about 7 million people voted. What was more important in your day?

comments.name: Barry Moskowitz
comments.body:
Though I always have been and remain a Democrat, I am dismayed that Gov. Hochul has won. I was never a fan of Mr. Blakeman, but it seems pretty clear that so-called Progressives, and perhaps their DSA allies, have secured a stranglehold on New York politics. It also seems clear that New York needs change in the political arena.

One of my big concerns is crime and disorder. I have heard people say that "crime is down," but that clearly is not the case. It is pretty easy to bury violent crime in overall stats that give a misleading impression, but look closely and we find that subway crime and other acts of violence have risen, especially against women.

Gov. Hochul reportedly once said that crime is a "perception," suggesting that people allow "anecdotes" to skew their overall impressions. That is not the case. I see the disorder every day. Stabbings, assaults on women, etc., are not made up or "isolated incidents"--they do seem to be happening, and the policies of Gov. Hochul and her allies do seem to be part of the problem. The summary release of repeat offenders, etc., makes life disorderly and dangerous--especially on the subways.

There will be those who insist that stats say what they clearly do not, those who actually call New Yorkers "fear-mongers" for reasonable concerns about the realities we see around us every day. They may mean well, but their baseless accusations contribute to the problems that afflict the city and state.

You also get protections that most people don't think about until it hits home: building codes, healthcare for women. There's a lot to love in NY; upstate and downstate! Congratulations to Gov. Hochul.

I hadn't heard this superstition, although I can confirm Thais are inclined to all sorts of beliefs most westerners find a bit odd.

I'll just chime in with what may also be part of the superstition: the abandonment of local customs and food for the dreaded assimilation of foreign ways.

Interestingly this works both ways: when I first lived in Malaysia in the early 1990s KFC was a recent import and popular as a date and business place, believe it or not.  

Local fast food, which abounds in Malaysia and Thailand to the north, tends to small stalls that each serve but one or a few dishes, with a central shared seating area between numerous food stalls.  The seating was rarely shaded or roofed, and one sweated or got wet when the rains came.

KFC offered A/C, unusual back then even in many homes, let alone a fast food restaurant.  The KFC in Penang had valet parking, and was considered posh as a result.  Surprised me to say the least.

Even our own food chain change overseas.  It makes sense locals would adopt their own versions and ideas about what we consider a basic and prosaic business.  I'm not surprised KFC came to be considered fancy in Malaysia and the cause of busy shifts to the north.  

I am surprised Thais would choose KFC over their own cuisine but even great food can become boring if one is too accustomed to it.  Still, I'd never eat at a KFC in Thailand, so many better traditional choices.  I'd be the guy bringing in a plastic bag of local curry sauce.

It also helped that McCain was the R nominee—the man who was a constant war monger (you recall the refrain bomb, bomb Iran). The pontification then became that this was a sea change in the electorate putting a black man in as president.  The analysts padded themselves on the back saying how the electorate had turned the corner and had become so much more tolerant. “The results come at a sensitive time for Israel, as it grapples with its inconclusive election and faces another possible round of conflict with Iran.”

comments.name: Semyung Oh
comments.body: I think that young people like me do not give up easily. In other's perspective when they look at me, they say wow that kid gives up too much. But I always get back to it even though it can be soon or like later. the reason is that young people sign up for a lot of things, thinking that they can handle it... they can't. For example I was in a church band now I am also in a school jazz band thinking that they would be easy to handle. I also am in chess club..... and tutoring...... takewondo...... and a dog to take care of...... also school itself. That may seem little but I always try to handle everything while doing what I love like playing guitar, reading BONE by jeff smith, watching mp100 by ONE, playing minecraft by mojang, playing untitled boxing game by drowingsome inside of roblox who was made by  David Baszucki and Erik Cassel. I dont really know why I listed who these things were made by though. Now lets talk adults. I think adults are just more thoughtful of what they o and what they sign up for. From past experiences, they know that signing up for things that have a whole gigantic side quest that you are required to do. So I think that young people do not give up, almost never, even though it seems like it and adults are just more careful of what they sign up for.... unlike young people.

comments.name: Madaline Brown
comments.body: Between younger and older generations, there’s a lot of things that can not be understood about one another. Older generations had things that younger generations don’t have or how older generations take longer to understand something new, such as advancing technology that the younger gens can pick up on quickly. If anything, older generations had differing experiences than the younger gens have today. Today, students can stay home and take online classes in a space they feel comfortable and safe in, while the older gens basically had to go to college. Even though the college experience differs from others, what matters more, especially to the younger gens, is that comfort of safely transitioning from one safe place in their life, to a life full of uncertainty and a whole lot of discomfort. In other words, a lot of younger gens prefer to put a lot of their focus on getting their degrees, than focusing on college experiences that could potentially cause issues for them. Beyond that, some students would most likely prefer to take a slower approach from the comfort of home to a world that pretty much forces uncomfortable interactions that are both necessary for future connections and how we grow as people in a world that is constantly changing. Overall, this is what I think some older gens don’t quite understand about the younger gens.

comments.name: Chase N
comments.body: The debate between the older and younger generations over the perceived laziness and privilege of the younger generation has been ongoing for hundreds of years at this point. The older generation argues that the younger generations (specifically, boomers and Gen X targeting Gen Z) are incredibly pampered and haven’t been met with any issues that would require the level of grit that the older generation had to output in order to succeed. The other side of the argument in favor of the younger generations highlights how society has changed significantly since the older generation has been the forefront of the population, and that there are new and unique struggles that younger people in society have to endure every day, such as the affordability crisis. My take on this is that the younger generations are not more entitled than their older generations when they were the same age; more likely than not, the ancestors of the older generations were probably saying the same things about them as well, showing the self-bias each generation has. The story of the college student dropping out is also simply there to spark argument between the two sides, as the student in question did not leave campus due to difficulty, but instead out of concern for her own safety. Not only that, but the student did not quit college altogether, but instead simply transferred to the online program, which will allow her to get the exact same degree without worrying about her safety whilst learning.

comments.name: Sara
comments.location: Glenbard West HS, Glen Ellyn, IL
comments.body: When considering if younger people give up to easily, or if older people valorize struggle, one major debate has been about how the younger generation is lazy. Some people argue that younger people dont give up easily, for example younger people are alway looking for solutions for major problems like climate change and Ai use, this shows that younger people do not give up so easily. However others including young people and older people would say that since younger people have it easier now, it results in younger people not pushing harder to try more.

comments.name: Gabe
comments.body: When considering young people leaving college early, one major debate is whether young people give up too easily or if older generations expect them to struggle too much. Some older adults believe young people quit too quickly when things get hard and need to learn to push through challenges. However others, including young people, argue that struggling isn't always necessary and that people shouldn't have to stay in difficult situations just to prove they can handle it.

comments.name: Ava
comments.body: I do agree that younger generations tend to give up easier, but there are sometimes good reasons. In other words, I think it is more normalized to stop doing something that is seen as challenging to you because of the fact that you might not want to deal with pushing through. But in instances like the article mentions, leaving situations that jeopardize one’s health and safety makes sense and shouldn’t be seen as weak. Overall, I think that the younger generations find things more challenging than maybe older generations did at our age, and with our life style being more laid back, it is normal for younger people to stop doing something challenging. Even then, that doesn’t give older generations the liberty to criticize a choice made by someone who is leaving a tough situation.

comments.name: Michael
comments.body: I believe that the decision to give up is never as straightforward as it may seem. On the topic of the generational divide in perseverance, there has been a lot of controversy. Young people argue that they quit situations that aren’t suitable for them because it’s better to leave than continue to struggle. On the other hand, adults contend that younger generations are “soft” and give up too easily. My view is that this debate is very nuanced. Older people are influenced heavily by their parents, who went through a lot more struggles than people do today, which causes them to be crude and think being tough is the most important. However, as mental health awareness continues to gain popularity, society encourages young people to step away from things that stress them out unnecessarily, like in the extreme case of the girl quitting college after two weeks. In conclusion, the debate is less of a dichotomy than it seems, and the two sides are both well warranted given the society they grew up in.

comments.name: Osme
comments.body: Yes, I think that young people tend to give up more easily. While the older generation contends that young people are weak hearted and don’t push through tough situations, I think it completely disregards a lot of the things that young people have already endured. The older generation will point out places where we are weak but I think they should have the desire to correct, discipline, or teach in the ways that they find acceptable. I think if they want us to be confident individuals, they need to be able to create the safe environment where we can thrive. Ultimately, it is up to both sides and both sides need to work together instead of trying to prove who’s “wrong” and who’s “right”.

The results also show that many Americans want to change and want their concerns about the economy and the government to be taken seriously.

comments.name: Reagan Westfield
comments.body: I am not the most educated on this, I do know that I support the opposite of Mr.Trump. This outcome is  progress against Mr.Trump, like gaining control over him in a way. They don't  technically control him but it has an influence over him. It's very important how Texas and Kansas voted democrat because of the fact that they almost always vote republican.  Kansas hasn't voted democratic since the great depression, that was like a long time ago.

comments.name: Ruthie Sarnoski
comments.body: Although I wasn’t shocked, I was still extremely happy and excited for the near future. Trump and the current Republican party have been making decisions that negatively impacted Americans for the past two years and haven’t been held accountable. Throughout Mr. Trump's term he’s raised prices while giving tax relief to billionaires like himself. This has affected everyday Americans, feeling the consequences of his decisions. There are other laws and decisions I can point to further proving my point that our President has failed the everyday American. The newly elected Democrats can now fight back against these life altering laws and decisions. These new changes don’t come as a shock to me, seeing that many lives have been affected negatively. I look forward to the positive changes the newly elected Democrats will bring.

comments.name: Avi George
comments.body: Obviously, the Democratic party winning is a very significant component of this election. A major factor that I personally feel is that very Republican states like Texas voted for the Democratic party. Over President Trump's reign the Republicans took over the senate for years. I am just shocked that now out of all times the Democratic party won. Even with Mr. Trump as president, people still need to change every now and then. I feel like now is the Democratic’s turn to run the senate for a couple of years.

comments.name: Brighton Norton
comments.body: I found it very surprising especially since Texas is a state known for the crazy amount of Republicans and Donald Trump supporters. Personally I'm not supportive of anything Trump has done and I don't support anything he's planning on doing, I don't trust him, especially not with my safety. My parents struggle with the constant raise of bills and people are constantly trying to get us to move and the raise in gas prices aren't helping with that right now. I very much agree with Peter Baker. I think people finally realized that what Donald Trump is doing isn't right and that Americans finally found their voice. I’m the kind of person that loves gossip so I can't wait to see what our country, the citizens, and our president does next.

comments.name: AMIAS STRAUB
comments.body: I am worried that we will maybe take part in some wars that will not end well. When you look at what the current government is doing, it makes me think we are preparing for something. What gives me hope is that in 2 years we might not have to worry, but maybe another bad president comes along but I am just hoping it is someone who thinks about how it will affect people and not the government. If that happens then we could hopefully make it out and not kill everyone in our world.

comments.name: Jonah S.
comments.body: The results of the elections made me shocked and extremely happy in different ways. I was extremely impressed and surprised that states like Texas, Kansas, Kentucky etc. I am elated to see the future of this nation, as the end of Donald Trump is closer than it’s ever been. This morning, I checked the news to see so many people elected as democratic. When I woke up and checked, I saw an entire article on the first blank. I can 100% see how democrats ended up basically destroying the election, due to recent gas prices, and the war in Iran. Donald Trump hasn’t done a single good thing for this country, so the fact that he and his republicans just got destroyed in this midterm election is extremely exciting. My one hope is that when the next election comes, a democrat is not only elected, but it’s a democrat that does things. Democrats don’t do enough when it comes to being elected for president. I would love to see a democrat that does lots of things for this country. I’d hope that we are to make peace with Iran once president trump is gone. The Iran war is the reason gas prices are so high. Gas has been raised in price by so much that I’ve seen $4-5 prices for gas just for one gallon. Before this entire Iran war I remember seeing gas from $1.50-3 for a gallon. It is insane to me that he even got elected in the first place. I’m truly elated to see these midterm results, because it truly shows that the country doesn’t like Donald Trump at all, as it turns out he is disliked tons.

comments.name: Darren
comments.body: During voting the details seemed significant even though I'm not really into that topic. It seems really hyped and cool about the win over the house especially since they usually lose and the comment Trump had. It was cool because all my friends were talking about it and they were really interested which made me wonder. At first I was completely confused with Texas turning blue and it was confusing and now I sorta understand and it's cool but I don't think I'm as invested in it like my friends.

comments.name: sisepuede
comments.body: Ah, I see...as trump well said throught the past few years"...the failing NYT"

comments.name: Jason
comments.body: The scary thing is how influential this paper is. The Times has been smart and caters to its base with no apologies. With almost no similar competition, editors and writers alike should hold themselves to a higher standard. Witness Woke v1. That was quite the disaster.

comments.name: Mikki
comments.body: I appreciate your investigative reporting and lifestyle stories. I’m happy to hear you are doing well. Keep up the great work.

comments.name: Marc Bungener
comments.body: I think you have a good strategy of reasonable pricing, which should get compensated with a larger subscriber base over time. After being forced into retirement and loosing corporate access I took a suscription but decided not to proceed with the Financial Time and The Economist because while they are quality publication their price is just way too high

comments.name: Scott
comments.body:
I am ok with paying for news, it's the cost of democracy.  Establish the highest standards and stick with them because our democracy will fail without this core function.  

News is not entertainment.  Keep the fun and entertaining stories, but the core must be careful professionalism.

comments.name: MSK
comments.body: Will someone please explain to me how in 2020 you had 3.4 million digital subscribers at $16.50 per month and now in 2026 you have more than tripled the amount to 15 million digital subscribers and yet have doubled the price of the subscription.

comments.name: digitl_bill
comments.body: I live in Maryland and consider myself a Washingtonian. After 40 years of reading the Washington Post paper and digital editions I came here. I am not disappointed.

comments.name: Annotate
comments.body: I'm glad the Times is profitable. A great newspaper. I hope we never lose objective news that will let us know that people like Trump exist. Thank you.

articles.title: The New York Times Adds 420,000 Digital Subscribers
articles.summary: After a slower second quarter, the additions in the third quarter keep the company roughly on track to meet its goal of 15 million subscribers by the end of next year.

comments.name: joe
comments.body: Hence the dumbing-down of "Global Warming" to "Global Climate change". In trying to reach the people who say "WHUT Global Warming?" every time it snows, seasonally or unseasonally, the phrase "Climate Change" was coined. The truth is that on the whole the planet is warming and weather in general has become less stable, resulting in extremes. For myself, I prefer Global Warming because it's true and it's in the face of the deniers who lack the intelligence or the integrity to admit it.

comments.name: Karen Norris
comments.body: The floodwaters may not solve the crisis, but we have had a particularly long and extreme drought. If El Nino is followed by an increase in normal rainfall, that would be a blessing. So aside from civil engineering solutions, I suggest lots and lots of prayers of every type and variety.

articles.title: The American Southwest Is Parched. Can the Recent Floodwaters Quench It?
articles.summary: A series of storms has added to reservoirs in the Colorado River basin, but the long-term water outlook remains bleak.

comments.name: The Oligarchy is Back
comments.body:
Optimistic! Hoping for 54 senate seats! All the money thrown into this tace against Democrats and still looking good. 

Only fear is how the Mad King who told us to pretend he's on the ballot will take it out on us for turning against him.

comments.name: JohnStewartMillian
comments.body:
The entire structure of government needs to think seriously, NOW, about how to prevent Trump from unilaterally dropping a nuclear bomb to appease his ego, because that is what will show him to his satisfaction that he has the power to do such a thing, when the rest of it is slipping away.

NOW.  Anybody who does not understand this danger does not get it.

comments.name: Dan C.
comments.body: We all should have bought stock in Heinz (ketchup) last week.  Tonight, tomorrow will be such fun!  SO glad to see SCOTUS shut Trump down again.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
As a statistician who knows how very unreliable predictions about the future can be: I want to know how tonight *went*.

Not "how it will go".

comments.name: jerry
comments.body: Paxton in Texas already said he wouldn't accept the vote result unless he wins.  This from the man sworn to uphold the law.

comments.name: Mr. Bentley
comments.body: Ossoff should replace Schumer now.

comments.name: Dinner
comments.body: This feels just like the 2020 presidential election and I think the  democratic electorate showed up with just as much passion. PLEASE 🙏🙏

comments.name: Jeffrey
comments.location: An 1885 Dutch Colonial in NW Portland
comments.body: Please, for the love of God, if we win tonight…. Shumer and similar neoliberal stooges have GOT to go. We thank them for their service but we need new blood. Otherwise it’ll be JD Vance in 2028.

articles.title: How Will Tonight Go? Here Are Races That Will Provide Early Clues.

comments.name: Kimberly A
comments.body: Trump has made his billions of dollars  so what does he care about this complete and total repudiation of his policies? He’ll focus on his egotistical construction projects which hopefully will either be stopped or torn down when he leaves.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: My perception of Pres Trump is that he loves to brawl but only if he sees himself as dominant and against a much lesser foe, and where there is, he at least believes, no cost to him personally. He only punches down where the opponent can’t hurt him. He wants his place in history and he wants to be adored. He may see cooperation with the Democrats as his path to secure both. His loyalty is to himself alone and has nothing to do with being Republican or Democrat. He will do whatever secures his personal desires.

comments.name: S Carver
comments.body: I also hope the Dems don't waste a lot of time on vengeance.  SCOTUS will protect Trump from accountability (and is IS old and not in great health, anyway).  There's so much work on the economy and social policies to be done - the focus should be on how to manage his use of veto power, and actually legislate.

comments.name: CC
comments.body:
This Op-Ed is what I've been thinking too. It's hard to be optimistic in the age of Trump. 

I would like to be very wrong.

comments.name: Madeleine Elster
comments.body: Congress has a lot of power, including appointing Supreme Court justices. Not only will trump not have the opportunity to put another person through, but there is a real possibility that some openings could occur w/in the next two years. Democrats could reclaim the court

comments.name: Scott Shuford
comments.body: Ah, what will the next two years bring? Ms. Cottle is undoubtedly correct that much scuffling will ensue. I expect, early on, there will be internecine warfare among the Republicans as the laughably obvious blame assignment is skirted like a large angry dog that must be brought to heel but whose bite is still feared. I further expect that the Democratic leadership will pursue a full array of legislative measures that they expect to fail by filibuster or veto but remind the American public that Republicans don’t want them to have nice things because - wait for it - billionaires need more money.

comments.name: Thomas Mac
comments.body: It’s time for Congress to take back its power and then some. Republicans can either get on board or pay an even higher price in two years. This time, the people really have spoken and they want action.

articles.title: Trump Has the Democrats Right Where He Wants Them
articles.summary: The president loves combat and chaos. He’s about to get more of it.

comments.name: Jaye
comments.body: Congratulations Florida, you’ve bested Texas this election for being the most misguided state in the union.

comments.name: Jon
comments.body: Moody is an intellectual and political light-weight and a Trump sycophant. Florida democrats look forward to retiring her from the Senate in 2028.

comments.name: ZR
comments.body: It was an impressive show for sure. I really thought Nixon could eek it out. We'll just have to come out stronger in another 2 years. We have a headstart on getting the word out now. On the bright side, DeSantis is gone and we have the chance to make real change and do good in the house and senate! Grassroots are back!

comments.name: Tom
comments.body: "her Senate campaign was not very visible, especially compared with Ms. Nixon’s." I live near Orlando, and except for some very generic looking billboards, the Nixon campaign was the one hardly seen. Did she have even one commercial on TV?

comments.name: Randy Kalkue
comments.body: Moody BARELY won in Florida.  Not a proud moment - more of a survival event.

comments.name: Alexander
comments.body: I would have loved to see a debate between them.  Sadly, it seems the republicans didn’t want their candidates having to defend all this chaos

comments.name: Scott OPottamus
comments.body:
Florida where I have lived for 70 years. Born in Miami to parents from NYC.  Friends and family mostly Democrats (except my WWII dad) Friends with Republicans. A good place to live. 
Then the Republican Party started siphoning off less informed, less skeptical folks with tough talk, bravado, “us against them,” and vindictive fear-mongering.  
It’s wonderful to see the Senate & House going Blue tonight. Bummed to see Donald’s and Moody being elected. But glad to see the move back to decency, normalcy, in other races. Moving back to the America I grew up in and never gave up on.  
I hope I awaken to a large font headline in the NYTtomorrow saying AMERICA WINS!

comments.name: 2cool2b kool
comments.body: Nixon will BE BACK and WILL WIN

comments.name: AH
comments.body:
While it may be very tempting to institute endless investigations, as well as an attempt to impeach Trump, the Democrats across the nation must focus on improving the lives of everyday Americans.

There will be an opportunity at a later date to hold accountable those who have damaged our nation on so many levels.

For now, though, the Democrats MUST focus on affordability, healthcare, energy & infrastructure, education, and the environment.

comments.name: Stefanie
comments.body: As great as yesterday was, I will have to see if this country can do the work needed to turn things around. Especially over multiple elections. I'm not sold on the capacity to fully end this awful era of governance.

comments.name: Liam
comments.body:
In my view, the Democrats didn't win it. The Republicans lost it.
The Democrats have a lot of lessons to learn from this. Their old schtick will not work anymore.

comments.name: Casual Observer
comments.body:
Trump and his unconditional support from Republican members of Congress handed Democrats a victory. Trump was drunk with feelings of entitlement and then lost control from his habits of acting on impulse with little due diligence. 

The Democrats should not assume that their proposed policies are what won the election for them. If they want to retain official authority, they are going to have to meet the voters half way and set aside the urge to enact what they think that voters should like.

comments.name: California Michael
comments.body: The landslide postponed, preferably ended, potential federalization of reproduction. The GOP's intention was to eliminate employers' pregnancy leave policies. Another GOP intention was to legislate fetal personhood rights in which state appointed attorneys would guarantee a fertilized egg or a fetus  be given rights over the mother.

comments.name: David Lindsay jr
comments.body:
Great discussion, thank you all very much. 
One high point, was your discussion of whether the Dems should get rid of the filibuster asap, or after the 2028 election.
So many good things to have to figure out.  E J Dionne, please don't sound scared to mention quickly the climate as an issue.  For some of us, it is the biggest issue.
Carlos Lozada, you have to fix your camera and microphone. Maybe your internet as well. Thel studio debates are so much better technically.
InconvenientNews.net

comments.name: JackCerf
comments.body:
Now that the dog has caught the car, there are three priorities.
First, enacting legislation that Trump will veto as a platform for 2028.  Second, using the appropriations power to tie his hands as much as possible.  Third, oversight.  Impeachments, which sucksall of the air out of the room and which lack a 2/3 majority for conviction, are a long way fourth.

comments.name: Lexicron
comments.body: Trump got what he's always wanted: He and his family are rich beyond belief--at our expense. Never forget that!

comments.name: Spartacus
comments.body: Douglas Adams, during his lifetime, constantly changed The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy as it moved from radio to book to television series. You won't see H2G2 fans complaining about faithfulness to the book or the radio series - Adams enjoyed teasing around with the story. I wish more fans of Dune and other properties worried less about using the books as a script and just enjoyed what is another artist's interpretation of the source material. Once I learned to do this, I appreciated Lynch's work for what it was, and I appreciate Villeneuve's work for what it is.

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: At last, the beige movie series comes to an end. I'm sure that there's loud sigh of relief coming from everywhere the movies were distributed.  I read the first two books in the series in the early 1970s and realized that it was a historical novel plot leavened with pharmaceuticals and comic book spirituality.  I saw the first movie in this series and decided the theme was beige.  Sand dominated the color palette and the characters were either boring or cardboard cutouts of villains.  Overall, it was like a 1990 computer case.

comments.name: Alan
comments.body: Chain estranged? That’s not in the book…..

comments.name: TB0
comments.body: Can't wait to see Nakoa as a sandworm!

comments.name: shawn
comments.body: If you don't understand Dune is a tragedy, you were reading what you wanted to, not what Herbert wrote. Paul knows through prescience that he will cause billions of deaths. Why does he choose to do so, anyway? The Fremen are on an unstoppable collision course with the reality of getting what you wanted won't give them what they wanted. Their naive belief is laid bare for us to see. Biotech might recreate the body but the person is lost forever (as Paul understands with Chania). The fates of nations and worlds are dictated by some leader's personal beliefs, needs, and foibles. We convince ourselves it is in our interest. For Paul, our hero, the best path is the bad lesser of many evils. Even though I read this at 10 years old, Herbert made me see the window dressing of heroics on top of tragedy.

comments.name: Hawk
comments.body: The same handful of actors are in every movie.

comments.name: HAR
comments.body: People understand that it can be hard to capture irony or sarcasm in translation from book to movie, or from voice to text; the words say one thing while the tone and expression and body language and context say the complete opposite.  "Yeah, *riiiiiiiiight*."  The issues in Dune are even more subtle, and explain why the 1984 attempt was so contentious: it LOOKS like the story is about Paul becoming a superhero, which misses the entire subtext that "superhero is dangerous and corruptible and maybe megalomaniac".

comments.name: Faustina
comments.body: That speech of Chalamet's in Dune 2 rousing the Fremen in some made up language was so legit. I hated when he slipped back into English because it broke the spell.

articles.title: ‘Dune’ Reunion: Timothée Chalamet, Zendaya and Friends Can Take the Heat

comments.name: KatLuver
comments.body: I find it outrageous that anyone rich enough, including government entities, can shoot equipment into space, to the moon or even other planets and leave their trash behind!! Our moon is covered with debris from various landings and just left there! Orbit of our earth has so much floating trash that a NASA monitoring group has to track it so new trash sent up doesn't collide. And now space trash is falling back to earth, threatening whoever gets hit?! And the elitism that of course, Europe and the US aren't in the trajectory of the decline...

comments.name: South Uist
comments.body:
Thank you for this reporting. I am wondering about the 1/2,100 odds of Swift causing an injury and take note of your (Ken's) remarks in the comment section, reminding us that there is only one known case of a person hit by space debris and this only involved incidental contact. As a result I now distinguish between space debris causing a) an incidental contact, b) material that causes a minor injury, c) then a serious injury and d) death. I would dismiss the first two categories and am curious if NASA did the same when they computed 1/2,100. 

"NASA estimates the odds that a piece of Swift would injure someone to be about one in 2,100."

comments.name: Out West
comments.body:
"Swift’s orbit is angled 20.6 degrees to the Equator. That means if you live north of 20.6 degrees north latitude or south of 20.6 degrees south latitude, there is no chance that a piece of a space telescope will fall on you."

It would have been interesting to see the effect of tumbling and ejecta during re-entry on cross-range deviation.  Surely, in the absence of a perpendicular delta-v component before entry, the inclination would be within +/-20.6 degrees...but I would not have been surprised to see the probable impact ellipsoid had some pretty significant width to it.

Aside: Back in the day, even The Sons of the Pioneers had quite a bit to say on this subject: "Seeeee them tumbling down...."

comments.name: Tyto alba
comments.body: That’s a pretty big chance. Compare it to winning a lottery.

comments.name: Mrmuring
comments.body: What happens to all the metals that evaporate into the atmosphere as it burns on its way down?

comments.name: Casey
comments.body: Twenty years beyond the original 2 year mission is an incredible run. Thank you for highlighting this scientific achievement.

comments.name: DazzRat
comments.body: If a chunk of metal survives reentry and hits someone on the ground at the object's terminal velocity, it's not going to "injure" them, it's going to obliterate them. If it remains big enough to have a blast radius or take down structures, then what is NASA doing? Having trouble conceiving a scenario where a piece of space telescope hurtles to earth and affects a person with an "injury."

comments.name: Ray Gunn
comments.body: It's a shame that the rescue mission was unsuccessful.

articles.title: A NASA Telescope Has Crashed Back to Earth
articles.summary: The space agency estimated that there was a one-in-2,100 chance that debris from the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory could injure someone on the ground.

comments.name: Kathleen
comments.body: The overwhelming customer support and China Star's customer floods reminds me of the old Lucy and Ethyl scene of the two of them in the chocolate factory stuffing chocolates down their pockets and into their mouths as the chocolate bon-bons came faster and faster down the conveyor belt. Funny TV scene, but probably no laughing matter for the newly overwhelmed China Star restaurant. If you are too young for this 1950's Lucy sitcom reference, watch it on YouTube. Hilarious!

comments.name: Ryan
comments.body: Respectfully, if they're too tired for success, perhaps retirement is the right move.  Better to go out when the going is good.

comments.name: theGrossman
comments.body:
I grew up in and around the restaurant industry I would have so many sugggestions for them but really it comes down to what to they see as an endpoint.  That is something they have to decide.  With no goal in sight they will simply be treading. water for years.  Here is something my Stepfather always told me.
There are three types of restaurants.
1. The family owned and operated. You work hard, there are not free nights and weekends and you'll hopefully make a living. this could be China Star.
2. One that opens with lots of hype and PR makes money in the first two years and then is sold for a profit.  this could also be China Star if they wish to sell out.  Although to a lesser extent.
3. And this was his favorite. The dilatant who opens a restaurant to show off, has a table in the back where they entertain friends and loves to walk around smooshing.  Why does he love this type.  Well he sold restaurant fixtures, and he told me he would be buying back everything he sold them at ten cents on the dollar.  He then held up a fork and told he. I have sold this fork four times.
Lickily, we know this is not China Star.

comments.name: Stephen Kerr
comments.body:
Fascinating article. An enjoyable and heart-warming read. It highlights the differing worlds of first versus second generation immigrants and the distinct goals they seek for themselves. The mother sounds wonderful, hard-working and possibly a little bit unused to change. The daughter has certainly kickstarted the business but at what cost? 

If anything, this article is about love. A mother's love for her daughter and the desire for her to have every opportunity her new country could offer, and a daughter's love for her tenacious mother who she wanted to help. It seems to me that they both love each other very much but what decision will they make about the restaurant when the mother eventually becomes too old to run it? Will the daughter continue to give up her career or will the mother take on more staff? I do hope we find out. 

A love story needs a happy ending.

comments.name: Melle
comments.body: My aunt's MIL used to own a big Chinese restaurant that she and the family basically ran 24/7. Legend has it that up until the day she died, she refused to sell it even though the family members were tired of it. Because the reality was that everyone stepped in to work at it year round - cousins running the cashier, washing the dishes, doing the prep. There was never a break. When MIL died, the restaurant was immediately sold but afterwards, my aunt always said - MIL loved that restaurant. Because it provided jobs for the family and the community, and so, it was so hard to let it go for her.

comments.name: Mishi
comments.body: Beautiful and thought provoking story. Mrs. Li represents many first-gen small restaurant owners I’ve met in California too. I hope she finds peace knowing she did succeed, if mainly in raising a caring, capable daughter who understood her struggle and was so generous with her time and love. Restaurants are excruciatingly difficult to sustain. I hope she delegates and doesn’t sacrifice her health for it.

comments.name: Alan Hughes
comments.body:
It must be heartbreaking to potentially lose a family business that has taken so much but also provided the next generation with security and a better future.

Unfortunately palates change and the Cantonese menu modified for locals possibly didn’t take into account that locals’ tastes have also changed and with a sizeable number of Chinese students other styles of Chinese cuisine were becoming more available. Those factors and the general cost of living impact on restaurants in general makes it a difficult climate to run a successful restaurant.

Edinburgh still has room for good Chinese restaurants and I hope that the family work out a solution that works for them.  In the meantime, we will pop along and support a deserving local restaurant.

comments.name: CC
comments.body: I live not too far from one of America's largest Chinatowns and like to visit. I wonder whether this story has played out here, too.

articles.title: Could a Viral Video Save Her Mom’s Chinese Restaurant?
articles.summary: Millions viewed Lisa He’s post about her mother’s struggling business in Edinburgh. But internet fame created its own complications — and obscured bigger questions.

comments.name: Just a Commenter
comments.body: Saudi Arabia, like billionaires, and Big Oil - should not exist.

comments.name: Space Age Robot
comments.body: Boeing guy here. Simulations of the terrifying plunge of this jet indicated it exceeded Mach 0.9 (or about 580-700 mph). The air frame of a Lear 60 is rated to 0.81 Mach number. This may explain why the tail section separated from the plane as the a/c exceeded its structural limits. One the a/c  became iced, the plane plunged (q-cornered) at which point recovery was impossible. The key was the icing, then a stall at high altitude. This was probably preventable if they had gone around the storm.

comments.name: John
comments.body: I am thinking of The Rehearsal season two right now. A young copilot and an older more experienced pilot. The CVR, if it survived, would be interesting to listen to - if the copilot had challenged the decision to go through a thunderstorm or remained quiet.

comments.name: Tom W
comments.body: I’d heard that there was no flight data recorded, but had a cockpit voice recorder. So perhaps somebody can glean something from that.  But I wonder if that CVR would , which survive that kind of impact. I was wondering if weather radar was working. Perhaps they put it on the MEL minimum equipment list for deferred maintenance.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
A horrific tragedy. 
A somber reminder that Mother Nature always has the final say.

comments.name: Not a sweetie
comments.body: That it took ATC to warn them not to fly through the severe storm area is telling. Severe icing can happen very quickly, especially in convective thunderstorms, and the co-pilot was already reporting ice buildup. A terrible tragedy. Condolences to all affected.

comments.name: Ralph LaForge
comments.body: Somewhat unusual to fly, apparently directly, into a thunderstorm.  They must have seen the storm's intensity on radar.

comments.name: Daniel B
comments.body: I agree that icing with loss of lift is the most reasonable explanation for this tragedy. This would also suggest human error as the underlying cause although more may come out of the investigation.

comments.name: Nope
comments.body: A horrific crash. So very sad. For many people, this is their worst fear realized.

comments.name: b fagan
comments.body:
Let's see. 
Trump freed a former president of Honduras who was sentenced to decades in a US prison after trial and conviction for charges related to large-scale drug smuggling.

comments.name: Sarah F
comments.body:
I discovered a few natural ways to manage this that the pharmaceutical industry will never pursue.

1. If I eat literally one bite of capers or sauerkraut, it's gone the next day?!  I've tried other fermented foods, but capers especially seems to do the trick. 1/4 teaspoon about every other day. Daily if severe.

2. Apple Cider Vinegar Rinse immediately eradicates the itchiness and reduces flakes. Usually once per month depending on severity.

In a 2-cup liquid measuring cup. Pour 1-3/4 C water and 1/4 C apple cider vinegar. Optional 2-3 drops of tea tree, lavender, mint, or rosemary essential oil as all these are naturally antifungal.  Clean/shampoo your hair and rinse out.  Then, pour apple cider vinegar rinse over head and work into scalp. Avoid eyes. Let mixture sit for 2 min.  Then rinse hair with cold water. Use conditioner only on the ends - at least a few inches from scalp. Fine for color treated hair too.

2. Beeswax Lip Balm on thicker patches behind ears and around edge of hairline.  The beeswax is naturally antifungal and seals the skin. 

3. Do not consume foods with Omega 6 and Omega 9 fats that cause inflammation.  Use only Omega 3 oils like Olive and Avocado that are anti-inflammatory.  If you cannot avoid it because those French fries are calling you, eat capers and/or sauerkraut in that same meal to mitigate.

4.  Sadly, do not drink beer...even 1 serving every couple weeks.  No more tequila.  No more rum.  BUT you can have hard apple cider or whiskey.

comments.name: Jen
comments.body: I suffered from dandruff since I was a teen and used prescription shampoos to treat it. Then, in a desperate attempt to stop cystic acne, I went gluten-free. Both the acne and the dandruff cleared up in 4 months and haven't returned since (I'm still gluten-free. These days I use shampoo and conditioner bars. My hair and scalp are the healthiest they've ever been (and there are no bottles to recycle).

comments.name: je
comments.body: I discovered, after hitting menopause and going on hormones, that the cause of my mostly lifelong dandruff was progesterone. Very badly itchy scalp and behind ears, huge flakes. Washing every day with a gentle shsmpoo (Aveda shampure) helps, but the only thing that cures it is no progesterone, which isn't an option. My daughters have this condition too.

A totally tonedeaf plea going to the 50% of parents who strain to pay full freight and are not eligible to send their own kids on an all-expenses-paid jaunt to Italy. So I'm not one of the super wealthy, but here's why I refuse to donate to my alma mater.  I graduated in the 1980's from a simple, no-frills bricks and mortar state college.  I received an excellent education at an affordable price.  

Fast forward to now and the school has since felt compelled to become a university and build new facilities rivaling the Taj Mahal in glitz and grandeur.  No surpise then that the tuiiton, room and board have increased exponentially over time.  

As an alumnus, I receive regular pleas to contribute to scholarship funds for the "less fortunate".  My consistent answer to the solicitations is, "if you hadn't spent the money on unnecessary grand and glorioud buildings and facilities, you'd not have to worry about squeezing alumni for scholarship donations".  They keep trying but I will never donate any $ to the school.  They created the problem, they need to figure out how to fix it.

The celebration was successful—as indicated by the spray of confetti, a hot swatch of reds coagulating against blues. The garlands sagged between the posts, like ancient gallows buckling under misshapen baubles of dead weight—attendees swaying, festooned in a danse macabre. It was a grand event, as innovative as a wedding could aspire to be. If only the bride had been written with a moment of consideration, the forensic flash would occupy the cover of a cherished album—passed down for generations.
But some brides are written in whimsical scripts by elegant hands adorned with chains of matrimony. And others are pressed through carbonless copy paper by calloused fists through chains of custody.

It's a new day in America!

What a great victory for Democrats and democracy! I'm thrilled to see the sweeping "Blue Wave" victories and so many capable, dynamic new leaders stepping forward. It's encouraging to see this kind of energy and momentum for a brighter future.

Now, it's time to ask: Who's really running the White House? I'd argue it's Stephen Miller and Russell Vought, with the president's support. Race-baiting, bigotry, and a lack of meaningful solutions to the problems facing everyday Americans didn't work.

But don't expect Vought and Miller to back down. They'll likely double down, making them two key figures to watch and hold accountable. The next two years could be a rough ride. Be ready.

For now, let's celebrate this victory, but don't let the momentum fade. Stay informed, stay engaged, hold our elected officials accountable, support these new leaders, and make your voice heard. comments.name: Victoria
comments.body:
I feel really uncomfortable with this decision to publish.  Moreover the writer does not mention what type of crime it was which makes me even more worried.  The desire to be published seems to be taking precedence over ethics. If it wasn’t an issue the author would not have written. 
Yes call adult protective services.  She is a danger to herself and others.  What if she turned the stove on.   And yes the building manager should also report it.

comments.name: Ken
comments.body: Memoirs always pose this type of challenge.  To be compelling they need to delve into the facts of the writer’s life which of course means sharing private details of loves, family members, etc.  I think it’s generally good form to give people a heads up and hopefully verify the facts, but this seems a bit different.  The brother was sentenced and went to jail.  It’s already in the public domain.  I agree w Appiah on this one.  Give the brother a heads up and listen to any concerns thoughtfully but then decide whether to publish.  He’s got no obligation to get an “approval” from his brother.

comments.name: Mari
comments.body: The memoir feels opportunistic and the LW knows it. Your conscience is in your gut, take its handy counsel when "doubts" arise that are more about letting yourself off a moral hook.

comments.name: P.J.
comments.body:
The LW has never discussed the crime and incarceration with her brother because it might have "destabilized" him, yet hasn't considered what might happen if she publishes the book & and he realized his life story has been told? 
It's really not your story to tell and I am surprised that your "mentors in the publishing world" haven't said so. 
Is this "memoir" actually presented as fiction with all names changed?  If not, leave your brother out of the book--though Googling could probably reveal the truth about the protagonists.

comments.name: Louise Stone
comments.body: Are you referring to legal consent?Aren’t “true crime” stories written all the time without the consent of the people involved?  In the US, I think writers/publishers risk lawsuits for defamation/libel if they publish damaging material that isn’t true, but they don’t need consent in advance to tell/publish the story. Is libel law different in England?

comments.name: James Igoe
comments.body:
Thinking about the decision, there are several paths forward, but the balance is on asking, even if you are denied:

- Publish, no approval requested
- Ask for approval; if no, remove
- Ask for approval; if yes, publish

Asking for approval and getting denied is functionally equivalent to publishing without approval. Otherwise, if you don't seek approval, you live with the 'Schrondinger's cat' of doubt, rather than a clear denial and moving forward anyway.

On a personal note, since it bothers you, you should ask. You are the one to live with your conscience.

comments.name: LV-426
comments.body: Even if you transformed it into a novel, everyone who knows you would know it was about your brother. You've been working on it for a long time, during a period that seems to have predated your brother’s dementia, and yet you never discussed it with him. I'm with the Ethicist on this one. It would be wrong to publish it without his consent. And maybe, in the course of broaching the subject with him, you would give both of you a chance to process these life-changing events from a different perspective, one last time. ?

Like a real life time machine. One had a spread about Argentina (?) a neighboring esctancia which had been given to a pastor as a gift for having helped the local community for a whole generation: huge amount of acres. And the same kind of mutton culture. Evan a romance: a young woman wandered down there and ended up marrying the son of the head of the estancia. Very romantic.  But the mother was a skilled watercolor painter and painted many wonderful canvases. The article was so hypnotic I could go over it time and time again, studying each photo endlessly. And even there " Tierra del Fuego" ? they now have tourism. 

Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: Hehaka Luta
comments.body: I see parallels between the Seneca Nation and my own Lakota Nation concerning matrilineal leaders and the traditional political power structures that existed before colonization. In my own nation we have had some very famous leaders, Sitting Bull, Crazy Horse, Red Cloud, among others known to Americans, but little known are the way they were chosen as leaders. At any given time we had not one but many elders in leadership chosen by merit, but women held the power to remove a leader if need be and held the power of veto ultimately. In this way there was a stability in balance. Our leaders earned eagle feathers and locks of hair from the women, a gesture that organically chose those we held the highest regard for. Women owned all property, the men and quite a few women too were hunters. Women were considered specifically sacred and powerful for the ability to create life. We didn’t lie to our constituents and the women elders suffered no fools. The Lakota women today are still extremely resilient in that respect. Unfortunately, the U.S. government prevailed in implementing their form of government that is as toxic for us as it is for them. If Americans truly desire to see our nations thrive alongside their own, honor our sovereignty and let us decide for ourselves how we need to be ruled and, perhaps, take a few cues from the 500+ nations already here who know your future because we’ve lived our past for tens of thousands of years, right here on this land.

comments.body: This is an interesting and important story!  To correct an incidental point, though, it is important to note that Alaska's ranked choice voting ("RCV") system is not a significant factor in that state's long processing time for votes. The key factors include Alaska's generous 10 to 15 day postmark grace period for mail ballots, numerous hand-counted precincts in remote rural precincts, and logistical (often weather-related) difficulties in transporting ballots from remote polling places to regional election offices.  When no candidate receives a majority of the votes, the "instant runoff" feature of RCV that produces a majority winner does add time, but this is rarely regarded as significant in other states and cities where RCV is used.  Republicans in Alaska dislike RCV because it has produced consensus-oriented winners in recent elections, and have successfully added RCV as a ballot issue in this election. One of the important results of 2026 will therefore be whether Alaska's innovative open primary - RCV system continues to serve as a model for those of us in the rest of the country who have had quite enough of hyperpartisan primaries and plurality winner-take-all elections.

comments.name: PolGuy
comments.body:
When "Almost Transparent Blue" came out in 1976, I was studying at a Japanese university, armed only with classroom Japanese. Opening the book was a shock: its colloquial cadence and raw subcultural slang were entirely foreign to academic texts. Wrestling through it was an ordeal, but I eventually finished it—and the unforgettable power of the characters and the unexpected elegance of Murakami’s prose have stayed with me ever since.

Clay Risen’s NYT obituary captures Murakami’s countercultural shockwave and late-career establishment embrace, yet it curiously overlooks "Coin Locker Babies." The piece highlights "Audition" and "Tokyo Decadence," making the omission of his 1980 tour de force all the more glaring. While I hesitate to declare a definitive “best” of Murakami—virtually everything he wrote possesses an electric, singular brilliance—"Coin Locker Babies"is an essential masterpiece.

Its frantic, unsparing depiction of trauma, rage, and institutional abandonment shows a novelist targeting, as he once put it, "one person reading alone." If you want to encounter Ryu Murakami at the height of his visionary ferocity, "Coin Locker Babies" is the one you must read.

comments.body: I'm in the Pac NW.  I had the luxury of not building on my property for 5 years after we bought it, so I was able to figure out where the best spot would be.  We bought a kit and my husband built the small greenhouse that has been a wonderful workhorse for me for the past 25 plus years.  Electricity and water, absolutely necessary.  Benches on north and south sides, a floor space at the back end to hold overwintering pots.  I grew hundreds of starts for our local plant sale for many years very successfully.  Grow lights are important since the veggie starts had to be of saleable size by sale time in early May.  I've been able to heat the space with just a small portable heater.  My only regret is that I didn't install a fan.  It gets too hot in there in the summer, so I have created an outdoor nursery bed along the north side of the greenhouse-I have to protect that from deer, which I manage to do.  My greenhouse is one of the joys of my life, useful beyond what I had envisioned.

We've had a 2 sided greenhouse for over 20 years in chilly Massachusetts.  South facing...Built into the L of the (ancient) house where an old fashioned porch used to be.  Double glass panels, ( a little pricey but have held up well), wood structure built by my husband ( the woodworker.)  Stone floor so water can seep thru to the ground.  Yes, it gets cold in the winter, so the door to the house is sometimes left open to the kitchen so heat can move to the gh. Small heat duct from cellar to the gh.  Gets down to 40sF routinely.  Summer: plants go out side under trees to avoid sunburn. 
A friend wanted a Gh too, and I advised the 2 sided type to save heating cost. She got a very fancy stand alone, and later told me she could hear the "ca-ching!' of the heating system midwinter.
Yes, I do grow orchids, various other houseplants, start seedlings, etc. One must carefully choose species, and varieties that will endure your conditions.  Happy growing!

comments.name: Jorge
comments.body:
Although this is a very big heist, it is remarkable that Binance was hacked using an old fashioned phishing attack that has been used by the North Koreans many times before, and should never have succeeded.

For example, in January 2015, the crypto exchange Bitstamp (then the world's largest) was hacked by a N. Korean hacker group, stealing more than 5,000 BTC -- worth more than $ 324 million USD in today's value.  (A detailed technical report of the hack was itself hacked from a dropbox account, and appeared on the internet.)

The hack proceeded over many months and employed sophisticated, individually tailored approaches to each senior manager at the company, starting with the CTO.  Top managers were targeted via email,  Dropbox, text and even paper mail to create legends, and the hackers thereafter exploited those ersatz relationships to obtain more information and ultimately, carry off the heist.

The electronic messages each contained a malicious VBA code, which upon activation, downloaded and gave obfuscated access to the hacker.  The big mistake then, as now, was to allow any manager access to the internet on a computer that also was tied to the hot wallet.  That should never happen.

Nor should any hot wallet be allowed to move that much value, that quickly, without a circuit breaker or even an alert.  Where were the safeguards?  All of these are well known, and easily implemented precautions.

This entire Binance episode may even be a cover for an inside job.

comments.name: J
comments.body:
There's a lot of points here that really begs the question of how legitimate this "hack" really was. First of all, as another just posted, an engineer used their work laptop for a job interview that included steps to download files to review and complete... I'm not the smartest person, but generally speaking most technical people would have known never to do this; especially on a heavily monitored end device. The so.called complex program from the hackers, was able to move funds between wallets, many, many, wallets with ease and at incredible speeds and didn't trigger any sort of odd behavior policies that would have certainly been in place..not to mention an infrastructure supporting this type of data would absolutely have a very strict and complex security system on the backend.
Granted, we're missing a lot of facts here, but I would love to see what a thorough log analysis of everything involved points out. Just saying....

comments.name: William
comments.body: Let's be clear. In the United Kingdom, these are called **Christmas adverts**, not “holiday ads.” They have been called Christmas adverts for generations, and there is absolutely no reason to impose the American habit of substituting “holiday” for “Christmas” on a country that has neither requested nor adopted it. Indeed, the annual unveiling of Britain's Christmas adverts has become something of a national institution, eagerly anticipated, discussed, dissected, and ranked by the public and the press, much as Americans await the commercials produced for the Super Bowl. John Lewis, Marks & Spencer, Waitrose, Sainsbury's, and other British retailers spend enormous sums creating elaborate miniature films, often featuring celebrated actors, memorable music, distinctly British humour, and a generous helping of sentimentality. These are not merely advertisements; they are part of the cultural ritual of Christmas in Britain. The irony of an American newspaper publishing an entire article celebrating this peculiarly British tradition while apparently being unable to bring itself to call it by its proper name is rather extraordinary. Britain has Christmas adverts. America may call its own seasonal commercials whatever it pleases, but there is no need to export American linguistic sensitivities across the Atlantic.
